items.title: Tanker Ablaze Off UAE as More Attacks Rattle Gulf Shipping
items.original_title: Tanker Ablaze Off UAE as More Attacks Rattle Gulf Shipping
items.summary: Vessels in the Strait of Hormuz, as seen from Musandam, Oman, July 31, 2026. REUTERS/Stringer A projectile struck the engine room of the Liberia-flagged crude oil tanker Dominica Prosperity off the United Arab Emirates on Wednesday, forcing the evacuation of all 22 crew members as emergency crews battled a fire aboard the vessel. The attack was one of four tanker incidents documented in the latest maritime security advisory covering the Persian Gulf and Strait of Hormuz, including a separate strike that left multiple seafarers injured. India’s Minister of Ports, Shipping and Waterways, Sarbananda Sonowal, identified the vessel as the Dominica Prosperity and confirmed that 19 Indian nationals were among the 22 crew members rescued by the UAE Coast Guard. In its November 12 advisory update, the Joint Maritime Information Center (JMIC) documented four tanker attacks since its previous report, including two in the Persian Gulf and two in the Strait of Hormuz. One of the incidents involved the tanker Fujairah Energy , which was struck by an unknown projectile while traveling eastbound in the Arabian Gulf on November 10. JMIC said the latest attacks bring the number of recorded maritime security incidents since March 1 to 181, underscoring the continuing dangers facing commercial vessels operating in the region.

items.title: GEODIS links Paris with northeastern Italy with new service
items.original_title: GEODIS links Paris with northeastern Italy with new service
items.summary: French logistics group GEODIS has launched a new rail freight service between Vicenza, in northeastern Italy, and Noisy-le-Sec, in the Paris area. The train is operated by Captrain and Hexafret, both part of SNCF’s Rail Logistics Europe, and currently runs once a week in each direction, with a second weekly departure planned from January 2027. The first train left on 19 October, GEODIS said in a press release. According to GEODIS, the service cuts CO2 emissions per shipment by 80% on average compared to an all-road diesel solution. The new line brings to northeastern Italy a solution that GEODIS already offers to companies in Lombardy, Piedmont and Emilia-Romagna through its connection departing from Novara. That service was launched in January 2022 and also terminates in Noisy-le-Sec, east of Paris. “Rail is an efficient mode of transport, especially over long distances, with much lower CO2 emissions than road transport”, said Jean-François Ancora, Managing Director of Captrain Italia. Bilateral trade in goods and services between France and Italy reached €136 billion in 2025, with Italy being France’s fourth-largest trading partner and France Italy’s second, according to GEODIS. With one weekly departure, the new line remains a modest service for now, but the planned doubling in January 2027 suggests GEODIS expects demand from Veneto shippers to grow.

items.title: Strong freight rates help Hapag-Lloyd profits soar, despite loss of market share
items.original_title: Strong freight rates help Hapag-Lloyd profits soar, despite loss of market share
items.summary: The recent strength in container spot freight rates drove a 480% year-on-year increase in group profit at Hapag-Lloyd in the third quarter, despite its liner shipping operations seeing flat volumes, indicating lost market share. Revenue in its liner shipping segment rose 25% year on year in Q3, “driven by a significantly higher average freight rate of $1,808 per teu”, compared with $1,413 per teu in the same period last year. Its third-quarter volumes reached 3.4m, marginally below last year and clearly below the global market – Container Trades Statistics (CTS) recently released Q3 data showed global volumes growing 5% year on year . However, Hapag-Lloyd CEO Rolf Habben Jansen said the period had seen exceptionally high levels of vessel utilisation, which had supported the higher freight prices. The carrier appeared to struggle on some of its core lanes – Asia-Europe volumes declined 5.7%, compared with Q3 25, to 927,000 teu, while its transpacific volumes also contracted, by 2.7%, to 1.2m teu. Hapag-Lloyd also reported a 35.1% increase in the average freight rate for these trades.

items.title: Spanish box terminals face cargo backlog after general strike
items.original_title: Spanish box terminals face cargo backlog after general strike
items.summary: Spain’s container terminals are beginning the task of recovering following yesterday’s general strike across the country that left box ships waiting at anchor after a slew of terminal closures – but the extent of the cargo backlog remains unclear. Container movements ground to a halt at Algeciras, loading and discharge was suspended at Valencia, and cargo operations requiring the support of dockers stopped at Barcelona, although essential marine services remained unaffected. Trade union confederation CCOO’s maritime-sector representative in Valencia for vessel operations, Francisco Martínez, told reporters: “There are no workers available, and there are no vessel operations.” And while one forwarder told The Loadstar the strikes had “zero” impact on their operations, AIS tracking data showed the 1,072 teu Contship Zen still at anchor off Valencia last night, with an expectation of berthing this morning. The scale and duration of any backlog will depend on how quickly terminals restore normal productivity, and whether carriers have had to revise their rotations or roll cargo, but requests by The Loadstar to glean this information from terminal operators today have fallen on deaf ears. Operations at both APMT’s Algeciras and Total Terminal International Algeciras were halted between 2am on 11 November and 2am on 12 November, bringing container movements to a standstill at one of the major Mediterranean transhipment hubs.

items.title: Wave of larger newbuild box ships a threat to the panamax fleet
items.original_title: Wave of larger newbuild box ships a threat to the panamax fleet
items.summary: The coming influx of larger containerships could render ageing panamax vessels commercially obsolete by 2030, while carriers’ efforts to renew smaller fleets threaten further capacity displacement. Jonathan Roach, analyst at Braemar, told The Loadstar the newbuilding programme was creating a substantial mismatch between vessels entering service and those approaching retirement. He identified the 4,000–7,499 teu segment as particularly vulnerable, with 428 vessels aged at least 20 years old against just 283 ships on order. Mr Roach said: “The ageing fleet is concentrated in the sub-panamax segment, while the orderbook is heavily skewed towards larger ships.” He warned that traditional panamax and post-panamax vessels could become increasingly squeezed, “potentially becoming obsolete by 2030”. Mr Pape-Leostic said: “In our view, this renewal will not be on a like-for-like basis,” and explained that carriers historically deploying vessels below 1,000 teu, could replace them with ships of 1,200 teu or even 1,800 teu. The figures suggest that the replacment of older vessels with larger ships could increase the global fleet’s carrying capacity without an increase in vessel numbers. Alphaliner’s data also shows the largest newbuildings dominating capacity additions, with 291 ships of at least 18,000 teu on order, representing 6.06m teu.

items.title: Chinese shipbuilder wins AHTS order from South American owner
items.original_title: Chinese shipbuilder wins AHTS order from South American owner
items.summary: Chinese shipbuilder Rainbow Offshore Engineering (ROC), part of Shenzhen-listed Jiangsu Rainbow Heavy Industries, has secured a contract to build an anchor-handling tug supply (AHTS) vessel for an undisclosed South American owner. The vessel will measure 71.95 metres long and 17.2 metres wide, with a bollard pull of 110 tonnes. Designed for deepwater anchor-handling and towing operations, the newbuild will feature a 300-tonne stern roller, shark jaws, and towing pins. Additional capabilities include FiFi-2 firefighting equipment, OSR-C1 oil spill recovery systems and facilities for supplying chemicals to offshore installations. The shipbuilder said the vessel could handle a wide range of offshore duties, from conventional platform supply and towing to emergency response and recovery operations. The order adds to Rainbow Offshore Engineering’s growing offshore vessel backlog. In November last year, the company announced a separate contract for multiple AHTS vessels for an overseas customer. More recently, ROC secured an order for one firm and one optional 4,000 dwt platform supply vessel in October. The shipbuilder has also been progressing its SPP40 platform supply vessel programme, with the fifth vessel in the series completing sea trials earlier this month.

items.title: Marine Platforms plans full takeover of former Technip pipelay vessel
items.original_title: Marine Platforms plans full takeover of former Technip pipelay vessel
items.summary: Nigerian offshore services contractor Marine Platforms is moving towards full ownership of the pipelay and heavy-lift construction vessel Zhong Fei Huan Qiu 1200 , formerly known as Global 1200. The company acquired a 51% interest in the vessel in 2025, with Chinese offshore engineering group DS Global retaining the remaining 49%. Marine Platforms now expects to take complete ownership within the next two years as it looks to strengthen its subsea construction capabilities in West Africa and other international markets. The vessel, also referred to as African Huan Qiu 1200 , was built by Keppel Singmarine in Singapore in 2010 and previously operated under Technip. The 162.3-metre vessel is equipped with a 1,200-tonne heavy-lift crane, an 800-tonne abandonment and recovery system, S-lay pipelay equipment and accommodation for 264 personnel. Designed by Ulstein, the DP2 construction ship can undertake pipelay and subsea installation work in shallow and deep waters. Damen upgraded the vessel in 2015, including improvements to its dynamic positioning and pipelay systems. Marine Platforms has identified the Mellitah Area D development as a potential assignment for the unit, alongside projects offshore Nigeria and elsewhere. The company has been expanding its offshore construction fleet, adding the deepwater diving support vessel African Pioneer to its operations in June 2025, which was mobilised for work at Chevron’s Agbami field offshore Nigeria.

items.title: EU’s Russian Arctic LNG Bill Hits €8.7 Billion as Yamal Faces Shipping Challenge Come January
items.original_title: EU’s Russian Arctic LNG Bill Hits €8.7 Billion as Yamal Faces Shipping Challenge Come January
items.summary: LNG carrier Vladimir Voronin off the coast of Honningsvåg on 15 April 2023. (Source: Courtesy of Kjell-Bendik Pedersen) The European Union paid an estimated €8.7 billion for liquefied natural gas from Russia’s Yamal project in the first 10 months of 2026, exceeding the estimated total for all of 2025, as the countdown to a ban on Russian LNG imports enters its final weeks. EU ports received 12.89 million tonnes across 177 cargoes between January and October, up 6.3% from the same period last year, according to an analysis by environmental group Urgewald using Kpler shipping data. The estimated bill is around 21% higher than the €7.2 billion calculated for all of 2025 . But the more immediate challenge for Yamal LNG, operated by Russian producer Novatek, is logistical. The EU ban on Russian LNG imports under eligible existing long-term contracts takes effect on January 1, forcing the project to redirect cargoes toward Asia just as winter ice makes eastbound navigation along the Northern Sea Route increasingly difficult. Yamal depends on 14 specialized Arc7 ice-class LNG carriers, which can operate in Arctic waters and return quickly from nearby European terminals. The January ban will not necessarily stop Yamal LNG exports, but it will remove the project’s most convenient winter market.

items.title: Russia shifts steel exports to Baltic ports from Black Sea in 2026
items.original_title: Russia shifts steel exports to Baltic ports from Black Sea in 2026
items.summary: Russian semifinished steel export flows have increasingly shifted away from the Black Sea toward Baltic ports in 2026, as disruptions to traditional southern export routes reshape shipment patterns and tighten the availability of Black Sea-origin material. There were no Black Sea steel loadings in either September or October, compared with 468,070 metric tons and 370,994 mt, respectively, loaded from Baltic ports. The Black Sea region had already seen a sharp decline in August, when loadings fell to 94,939 mt across three voyages, while Baltic ports handled 341,399 mt across 10 voyages, S&P Global Commodities at Sea(opens in a new tab) data showed. In 2025, Black Sea ports handled 5.687 million mt compared with 6.516 million mt through the Baltic, giving the Baltic a 53.4% share of combined volumes. In the available 2026 data, Black Sea loadings total 1.754 million mt compared with 4.335 million mt through Baltic ports, raising the Baltic share to 71.2%, according to S&P Global Market Intelligence’s Global Trade Analytics Suite data. Black Sea shipments fell from 346,109 mt in March to 188,291 mt in April and 96,879 mt in May. “We are planning 100,000-120,000 mt for seaborne exports to Turkey/Egypt through Baltic Sea ports [of billets], to be produced in November for December delivery.

items.title: Pacific Environment Welcomes Ulsan Port’s Commercial e-Ammonia Bunkering Milestone
items.original_title: Pacific Environment Welcomes Ulsan Port’s Commercial e-Ammonia Bunkering Milestone
items.summary: On October 25–26, Ulsan Port Authority (UPA), together with Lotte Fine Chemical, HD Hyundai Heavy Industries, Shinheungsa, and Eastern Pacific Shipping (EPS), supplied 800 tonnes of renewable energy-based e-ammonia to Terra Clove, a newly launched 93,000 m3 Very Large Ammonia Carrier (VLAC) at Ulsan Port. The fuel was supplied through a Port-to-Ship (PTS) bunkering system connecting the port’s onshore infrastructure directly to the vessel. The operation represents Korea’s first demonstration of commercial-scale ammonia bunkering at a domestic port. Reactions from Ulsan Port Authority BYEON Jaeyoung, President of Ulsan Port Authority, said, “This project was a clear demonstration of the importance of strong collaboration and coordination with relevant authorities and industry partners to advance ammonia bunkering operations at Ulsan Port and in South Korea,” And he added, We will continue to promote ammonia ship fuel supply in cooperation with related institutions and companies to ensure Ulsan Port establishes itself as a hub for supplying eco-friendly ship fuel.” KIM Byunggu, Director of the Sustainable Energy & Environment Department at Ulsan Port Authority, added, “We will strengthen cooperation with industry partners and related organizations to expand ammonia bunkering infrastructure and support the transition to cleaner shipping fuels.” Ulsan Port Authority is also taking concrete steps to accelerate the adoption of alternative marine fuels through financial incentives and port infrastructure support.

items.title: Monjasa adds five sister tankers in major fleet renewal deal

items.summary: Global oil and shipping group, Monjasa is adding five sister tankers to its fleet in the company’s largestever tonnage acquisition, strengthening its activities in West Africa and providing greater flexibility across its global marine fuels supply operations. The deal comprises five 16,621-dwt product tankers from German shipowner Bernhard Schulte, as part of the ongoing fleet renewal strategy and continued investments in reliable supply infrastructure. The first four tankers, Monjasa Tracer, Monjasa Tuner, Monjasa Twister and Monjasa Tracker have already been delivered and deployed in West Africa and Northwest Europe. Largest-ever tonnage acquisition in Monjasa “We are always looking at fleet renewal opportunities, but we are also very selective about where we invest. Five sister vessels bring operational benefits The acquisitions follow another active year in which Monjasa completed a total of 16,741 marine fuels operations in 2025. With a deadweight capacity of 16,621 tonnes each, the newly acquired vessels will strengthen the company’s ability to serve different markets and adapt its fleet deployment to changing patterns in global demand. The fact that these are five sister vessels is particularly attractive to us. Initially, the new tankers will strengthen Monjasa’s West African operations, while also providing opportunities for commercial freight trading and future deployment elsewhere in the group’s global supply network.

items.summary: The Maritime and Port Authority of Singapore (MPA) and NUSX, the entrepreneurial heart of the National University of Singapore (NUS), announced the winners of the 10th PIER71 Smart Port Challenge (SPC) at its Grand Finale today. From AI and robotics innovation for ships, to port automation and maritime cybersecurity solutions, this year’s Challenge attracted a record 586 proposals from 281 start-ups across 39 countries (see Annex A), reflecting growing international interest in developing technology solutions for the maritime industry. Showcasing Maritime Innovation at SPC 2026 Ocean Intelligence from Australia won the Top Start-up Prize for its AI-powered voyage optimisation platform that incorporates ocean currents, weather conditions and vessel characteristics to identify more fuel-efficient routes. Four thematic prizes of S$10,000 each were also awarded: Underwater Solution from South Korea received the Digitalisation Prize, sponsored by RINA; Ocean Intelligence from Australia received the Maritime Green Technologies Prize, sponsored by OCBC; Trunk Technology (Beijing) from China received the Smart Port Prize, sponsored by PSA Singapore and PSA Ventures; and Vueron Technology from South Korea received the Smart Shipping Prize, sponsored by American Bureau of Shipping (ABS). Participants worked on solutions addressing 20 innovation opportunities identified by maritime companies across digitalisation, maritime green technologies, next generation port and smart shipping.

items.title: Korea and China vie to lead ammonia-fueled shipping market
items.original_title: Korea and China vie to lead ammonia-fueled shipping market
items.summary: Korean and Chinese shipbuilders are locked in a battle of pride over ships that carry ammonia. Korea is highlighting the world’s largest ammonia “propulsion ship,” while China is rolling out an ammonia “carrier.” The situation signals fierce competition for the next-generation ship market. According to the shipbuilding industry on the 3rd, HD Hyundai Heavy Industries said last month it built the “world’s largest” ammonia propulsion ship. Earlier in June, Jiangnan Shipyard under China’s largest shipbuilding group, China State Shipbuilding Corporation (CSSC), delivered to EPS an ultra-large ammonia carrier (VLAC; Very Large Ammonia Carrier) with the same cargo tank capacity as HD Hyundai Heavy Industries and described it as the “world’s largest” VLAC. Earlier, in April, HD Hyundai Heavy Industries completed construction of its first ammonia propulsion ship, the 46,000 ㎥ mid-size ammonia-fueled gas carrier Antwerpen, and delivered it in June to the owner (Exmar LPG France).

items.title: Why shipowners might be better off sharing profits than taking on debt
items.original_title: Why shipowners might be better off sharing profits than taking on debt
items.summary: Traditional loans demand repayments regardless of freight markets. Earnings-sharing structures offer a different proposition: investors participate in a vessel’s fortunes while owners retain control. Captain Vikas Pandey from Shipfinex explains. Small and mid-sized owners, who by one industry estimate own up to 60% of the world’s ships, still meet low advance ratios on older tonnage, higher margins, or alternative lenders asking for equity kickers and profit participation on top of interest. Earnings-sharing tends to make sense where bank debt is unavailable or priced close to equity; where the vessel has visible employment, such as a period charter, that investors can underwrite; where the owner needs to protect liquidity through the cycle; or where equity is locked in an unencumbered vessel that the owner wants to release without selling. Before signing, owners should settle the definition of net earnings and deductible costs, the treatment of off-hire and drydocking, reserve funding, the term and any cap on investor returns, buy-back rights, and what happens on a sale or total loss. Where a first-priority registered ship mortgage is in place, the mortgagee’s consent is required and investor distributions rank behind debt service. Debt remains the cheapest capital in shipping for owners who can get it on good terms.

items.title: NYK charts the great reshuffling of global commodity trades
items.original_title: NYK charts the great reshuffling of global commodity trades
items.summary: One of the world’s largest shipowners has given its take on where it sees the gas, dry bulk, and tanker markets heading in the coming years. The global VLCC fleet will see a significant expansion despite the extraordinary earnings currently being enjoyed by tanker owners, with Japanese shipping giant Nippon Yusen Kaisha (NYK) forecasting the delivery of approximately 290 supertankers between 2026 and 2029. NYK’s research group unveiled its latest shipping market outlook yesterday, predicting that the active VLCC fleet will increase from 909 vessels at the end of 2025 to 1,082 by the end of 2029, a rise of 19%. The forecast assumes a substantial number of ageing vessels will leave the market, but deliveries are expected to be comparable to those witnessed during the shipping boom of the 2000s. NYK’s research also anticipates a fundamental restructuring of global commodity trades over the coming decade. Seaborne iron ore volumes are forecast to decline from 1.65bn tonnes in 2025 to 1.40bn tonnes in 2035 as Chinese steel production contracts. Coal shipments are forecast to fall from 1.33bn tonnes to 1.04bn tonnes over the same period, with thermal coal accounting for most of the decline. LNG is heading in the opposite direction, with seaborne volumes expected to climb from 433m tonnes to 622m tonnes by 2035.

items.title: Bunker prices plunge 20%
items.original_title: Bunker prices plunge 20%
items.summary: Bunker prices have plunged by as much as 20% in less than two weeks as hopes of an easing of the Iran conflict send oil markets tumbling, offering shipowners some relief from what is still expected to be the most expensive year for marine fuel on record. Singapore very low sulphur fuel oil (VLSFO) was assessed by Ship & Bunker at $814.50 a tonne yesterday, down from $1,019.50 on October 30, a drop of $205, or 20.1%. The retreat represents a saving of $615,000 on a 3,000-tonne bunker stem compared with the end of last month. Splash reported on November 3 that Singapore VLSFO had climbed back above $1,000 a tonne for the first time since March, with the Iran conflict having almost doubled bunker prices since February. Despite the latest retreat, Singapore fuel remains approximately 56% more expensive than immediately before the war began on February 28. Meanwhile, Clarksons Research has put shipping’s total bunker bill this year at a record $220bn. Speaking at the IBIA Annual Convention in New York yesterday, Clarksons Research managing director Steve Gordon estimated the global bunker market at 290m tonnes annually. Fuel demand is rising again despite modern ships being around 50% more efficient than vessels built 15 years ago.

items.title: Singapore Strait robbery spike sparks fresh security warning
items.original_title: Singapore Strait robbery spike sparks fresh security warning
items.summary: A sudden resurgence in robberies aboard merchant ships in the Singapore Strait has prompted regional maritime security authorities to issue an urgent warning, with three vessels boarded in nine days and one seafarer injured. The ReCAAP Information Sharing Centre issued an incident alert yesterday following attacks on two bulk carriers and a tanker between November 2 and 10, warning that further incidents are possible. All three robberies occurred in the eastbound lane of the Traffic Separation Scheme, within approximately 3.2 nautical miles of each other. The first incident involved the bulk carrier Star Calypso, boarded at 2125 hrs on November 2. The second, involving the bulk carrier APJ Priti 2, took place late on November 4, followed by an attack on the tanker Salsa in the early hours of November 10. The latest incidents bring the number of robberies reported in the Straits of Malacca and Singapore this year to 28. ReCAAP is urging Indonesia, Malaysia and Singapore to intensify patrols and surveillance, improve coordination and share intelligence to identify and arrest those responsible. Shipmasters have been advised to maintain heightened vigilance, particularly during darkness, and strengthen preventive measures, including CCTV coverage of potential boarding locations. The organisation is also encouraging vessels to report suspicious activity immediately and use its digital reporting and incident mapping systems when assessing voyage risks.

items.title: US Treasury may allow purchase of sanctioned tankers on case basis
items.original_title: US Treasury may allow purchase of sanctioned tankers on case basis
items.summary: The US Treasury Department may allow companies to buy sanctioned shipping vessels and return them to legitimate shipping on a case-by-case basis, according to a government source and a person with knowledge of the matter. “Treasury may consider proposals from legitimate shipping actors to purchase and restore shadow fleet vessels to the licit shipping industry on a case-by-case basis,” a US official told Platts, part of S&P Global Energy. This approach “ensures that no sanctioned person receives any benefit, and reduces the size of the fleet overall, while helping address pressures on the global energy market,” the US official said. Another source with knowledge of the matter said Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control could be targeting 50-80 sanctioned tankers owned by non-sanctioned companies. At the end of September, there were a total of 1,225 tankers sanctioned by the US, UK or EU, S&P Global Commodities at Sea(opens in a new tab) said in an Oct. Of those, 560 were sanctioned by the US. In 2026, 41 shadow-fleet crude tankers entered compliant trade through Oct. 20, with 68% remaining fully compliant so far, compared with just 17.5% of vessels that remained compliant in 2025.

items.title: ENGINE: Europe & Africa Bunker Fuel Availability Outlook
items.original_title: ENGINE: Europe & Africa Bunker Fuel Availability Outlook
items.summary: Northwest Europe Fuel availability remains tight in the ARA ports for prompt delivery dates, and buyers are recommended lead times of 5-7 days to get good coverage from suppliers and secure deliveries at competitive prices, a trader told ENGINE. The ARA’s independently held fuel oil stocks have averaged 2% higher in November so far, compared to October’s monthly average, according to Insights Global data. Fuel oil stocks have increased by 57% from May, when they hit their lowest level in more than a decade. Prompt fuel availability is generally tight in the Gibraltar Strait ports, with buyers advised lead times of 6-7 days to secure any fuel grade. Fuel availability is tight in the Canary Islands hubs, with buyers advised lead times of around 7-10 days for most deliveries, a trader told ENGINE. items.summary: Ivar Hansson Myklebust, chair and CEO of Norway’s Belships, believes the shipping industry continues to underestimate the growth potential of developing economies. Ahead of his appearance at Geneva Dry 2027, he discusses China’s changing trading patterns, fleet supply and the opportunities emerging across minor bulks. A changing China, resilient emerging economies and a relatively predictable fleet supply picture will be among the biggest themes shaping dry bulk shipping when the industry gathers in Geneva next April, according to Ivar Hansson Myklebust. China’s changing role in dry bulk shipping is another development he believes deserves closer attention. On technology, Myklebust sees opportunities less in revolutionary developments than in improving everyday shipping processes, from maintenance planning to freight collection. Myklebust will join the Minor Bulks panel at Geneva Dry on Wednesday, April 28, alongside Emilie Nourry of Eramet, Malgorzata Gill of Holcim Trading, S.K. For Myklebust, the value of Geneva Dry lies in bringing together the different sides of the commodities shipping business. “And meeting market participants from all sides of the business is never a waste of time.” Geneva Dry 2027, the world’s premier commodities shipping conference, takes place at the Hotel President Wilson on April 27 and 28 with organisers today unveiling limited special discount rates at the five-star hotel for signed-up delegates.

items.original_title: Russian Diesel Faces U.S. Buyer Resistance Despite Trump Sanctions Waiver
items.summary: HOUSTON, Nov 11 (Reuters) – US companies are unlikely to import Russian diesel as a tanker full of the fuel idles off the US Eastern Seaboard, experts said, despite President Donald Trump’s temporary waiver of some sanctions on Moscow’s fuel exports. Banks are likely to be reluctant to finance US deals for Russian diesel, the experts said, noting there are legal questions about whether the president’s waiver is enough to allow for the imports. There are also operational challenges, because importers would need to blend the Russian diesel to meet US heating oil specifications. That is down 20 cents a gallon from $6.33 the day that Trump waived the sanctions in October but up 63% from $3.76 before the US-Israeli war on Iran began in late February, according to AAA data. A Trump administration official said the temporary waiver was in compliance with all applicable laws. Banks are unlikely to finance deals related to a Russian diesel trade, which could violate sanctions in other countries, said David Tannenbaum, director of sanctions consultancy Blackstone Compliance Services and a former US Treasury sanctions specialist.

items.summary: FILE PHOTO: Oil/Chemical Tanker "Bald Man" at the Port of Fujairah, as the U.S.-Israel conflict with Iran limits marine traffic in the Strait of Hormuz, in Fujairah, United Arab Emirates, May 6, 2026. REUTERS/Amr Alfiky/File Photo International Maritime Organization (IMO) Secretary-General Arsenio Dominguez has called on governments to step up enforcement of international maritime regulations in the Strait of Hormuz, warning that unsafe shipping practices are adding to the risks facing seafarers amid the ongoing conflict. In a statement issued Wednesday, Dominguez raised concerns about vessels transiting the strategic waterway without complying with basic international safety requirements, including provisions of the International Convention for the Safety of Life at Sea (SOLAS). The warning comes as commercial shipping continues to face attacks in and around the Strait of Hormuz, where the IMO has now verified more than 130 incidents involving merchant vessels since the conflict began on February 28. The IMO chief specifically cited reports of substandard vessels, ships concealing their IMO identification numbers, vessels operating under fraudulent registrations or false flags, and other unsafe practices. The latest appeal follows last week’s meeting of the IMO Council in London, where member states called for stronger protections for seafarers and reiterated that vital shipping lanes must remain open, safe and secure.

items.title: UK Launches ‘Atlantic Net’ to Track Russian Submarines and Protect Undersea Cables
items.original_title: UK Launches ‘Atlantic Net’ to Track Russian Submarines and Protect Undersea Cables
items.summary: The UK is moving ahead with a £90 million investment in autonomous underwater systems, advanced sensors and artificial intelligence to strengthen the Royal Navy’s ability to track Russian submarines and protect critical infrastructure in the North Atlantic. The initiative, known as Atlantic Net, is the first operational phase of the Royal Navy’s broader Atlantic Bastion programme, which aims to combine crewed warships and submarines with autonomous systems to improve underwater surveillance and counter potential threats to subsea communications cables, energy networks and shipping routes. The UK Ministry of Defence announced the investment Tuesday during the International Sea Power Conference in Oslo, Norway, alongside a framework agreement with UK-based marine robotics company Ocean Infinity Solutions. The system will combine underwater sensors, uncrewed platforms, communications technology and AI-powered data analysis to detect and track potentially hostile submarine activity. The programme is expected to become operational in 2027, according to UK Defence Minister Luke Pollard, who outlined the plans in a speech in Oslo. “This investment gives the Royal Navy new technology to find threats earlier and protect our critical infrastructure, while also backing British business.” The investment comes amid growing concern among European governments and NATO allies over the vulnerability of underwater infrastructure, particularly communications cables and energy connections that are essential to both civilian economies and military operations.

items.summary: In recent months, a daily review of container terminal utilisation levels has become something of a ‘must-read’ for supply chain planners seeking to understand where boxes may be delayed, and for how long. That remains an art rather than science, but indicates how the container shipping industry has experienced something of a paradigm shift into an era in which waves of mega-congestion ripple across the port and shipping system. Terminal occupancy levels – ie, how many containers are sitting in a yard awaiting either a truck or loading on a vessel – continue to sit way above what these facilities were designed to handle. Some of this is beyond terminal operators’ control – they have no say over when vessels arrive, or how delayed they might have been at the previous port; while wars, weather, and other disruptive events are in the hands of the gods – or people who think of themselves as such… However, in the spirit of supply chain resilience, they could be far better prepared to tackle congestion when it arises.

items.title: UK taps Ocean Infinity for subsea security push
items.original_title: UK taps Ocean Infinity for subsea security push
items.summary: UK-based marine robotics specialist Ocean Infinity has been selected as the Royal Navy’s commercial mission partner for a new underwater surveillance programme backed by an initial £90m ($120m) investment. The company will work with the Royal Navy to develop Atlantic Net, a network of autonomous maritime systems, underwater sensors and artificial intelligence designed to monitor the North Atlantic and protect critical subsea infrastructure. The programme forms the first operational phase of the Royal Navy’s wider Atlantic Bastion initiative, which aims to combine crewed warships with autonomous and remotely operated systems. The Ministry of Defence said the framework agreement with Ocean Infinity would pave the way for the £90m investment and support almost 200 skilled jobs. The system is expected to become operational in 2027, providing Royal Navy warships and Astute-class submarines with earlier warnings of potential underwater threats. Ocean Infinity will work with specialist partners to combine maritime platforms, underwater sensing, communications, remote operations, and data services into a persistent surveillance capability. The company operates a fleet of remotely operated and lean-crewed vessels used for offshore surveys and subsea operations. One of its Armada vessels participated in Royal Navy trials earlier this year. The initial programme will also draw on UK technology suppliers, with much of the equipment expected to come from small and medium-sized businesses.

items.title: Monjasa seals biggest-ever fleet deal with five-tanker swoop
items.original_title: Monjasa seals biggest-ever fleet deal with five-tanker swoop
items.summary: Danish bunker supplier and shipowner Monjasa has acquired five sister product tankers from Germany’s Bernhard Schulte in its largest-ever fleet deal, strengthening its marine fuels operations in West Africa. The Fredericia-based group has picked up five 2010- and 2011-built tankers of around 16,500 dwt each. The purchase price has not been disclosed. Four vessels, renamed Monjasa Tracer, Monjasa Tuner, Monjasa Twister and Monjasa Tracker , have already joined the fleet and are trading in West Africa and Northwest Europe. The fifth, Monjasa Trigger , is set to follow by the end of November. The acquisition takes Monjasa’s owned fleet to 20 tankers, alongside around 10 ships on time charter. Group chief executive Anders Østergaard described the purchase as the company’s largest single tonnage acquisition, highlighting the benefits of taking on five identical vessels with established operating costs and technical requirements. “Finding five sister vessels of this quality, at competitive market terms and with an operating profile that fits our existing fleet, is not something you come across every day,” he said. The deal builds on Monjasa’s earlier tanker investments in West Africa, including the 2023 acquisition of the 68,589 dwt Monjasa Leader and the 13,051 dwt Monjasa Refiner , which were brought in for floating storage and bunker supply operations, respectively.

items.title: Coal’s new world order takes shape
items.original_title: Coal’s new world order takes shape
items.summary: Coal’s changing trade map is creating winners and losers across dry bulk shipping in 2026, with Indonesian exports retreating, southern African shipments setting records and Asian import demand increasingly fractured. Clarksons Research forecasts seaborne coal trade will edge up just 1% this year to 1.343bn tonnes. Beneath that modest increase, Indonesian exports are projected to fall 6% to 496.9m tonnes, while Australian shipments climb 4% to 371.3m tonnes. BIMCO reports coal imports dropped 7% in the first ten months despite coal-fired electricity generation rising around 9%. BRS says coal inventories at power stations were equivalent to only 5.9 days of consumption, against 14.7 days a year earlier. Supramaxes have been hardest hit, with Indian-bound coal volumes falling 16%, compared with a 4% decline for panamaxes. October offered the first signs of a turn, with Indian seaborne coal arrivals rising 7% year-on-year. However, BIMCO expects only a limited import recovery in 2027 as domestic mining grows.

items.title: Hapag’s standalone Asia-Mexico string adds another spoke to Gemini hub network
items.original_title: Hapag’s standalone Asia-Mexico string adds another spoke to Gemini hub network
items.summary: Hapag-Lloyd has presented AMX, its new Asia–Mexico service, as standalone: its own ships; its own rotation of Ningbo-Qingdao-Busan-Ensenada-Manzanillo-Lázaro Cárdenas-Ningbo; launching in January 2027. Standalone is the word the press release leans on, and it is the one worth questioning. AMX is standalone the way a spoke is standalone – Hapag owns the vessels, but it can only fill an 8,000 teu ship on this run because the Gemini hub network it operates with Maersk gives the cargo somewhere to come from. The hub-and-spoke network it now runs with Maersk supplies the missing pieces – balancing cargo through the Gemini hubs and relay connections onward, so AMX does not have to source a full, self-sufficient ship at Asian load ports. The simple answer to ‘why standalone’ and ‘why 2027’ is that the network to support a self-controlled spoke only recently came together. Each is an owned loop made to clip onto the Gemini backbone, and the method is consistent — control the vessel, fill it through the hubs. That slice is not small: I estimate Hapag’s allocation on MSC’s loops is worth around 8,375 teu of nominal vessel capacity, call it some 7,000 teu of usable space for its customers once a ship is realistically loaded.

items.title: Panama Canal turns the taps back on
items.original_title: Panama Canal turns the taps back on
items.summary: The Panama Canal has raised its daily transit capacity to 34 vessels and increased the maximum allowable draft for neopanamax ships to 50 ft, marking another significant easing of restrictions following an exceptionally wet October. The Panama Canal Authority (ACP) confirmed that an additional booking slot for super-category vessels at the original panamax locks would increase their daily allocation from 18 to 19. Total availability now stands at 24 slots through the panamax locks and 10 through the larger neopanamax locks, up from a combined 33 previously. The maximum neopanamax draft has meanwhile increased from 49 ft to 50 ft (15.24 m), effective immediately and until further notice. Data compiled by Ursa Shipbrokers showed Gatun Lake averaged 85.80 ft (26.15 m) during October, just 0.15 ft below its historical average and more than 6 ft higher than during the drought-stricken October of 2023. Rainfall across the canal watershed during the first 29 days of October was 8.4% above the 30-year average and 83.6% greater than the corresponding period three years ago. The turnaround is particularly striking given the dire outlook during August, when weak rainfall and a strengthening El Niño forced authorities to slash daily booking capacity to 32 vessels and impose tighter draft restrictions.

items.title: Russian crude exports fall on G7 tankers as Greek operators flee for better earnings
items.original_title: Russian crude exports fall on G7 tankers as Greek operators flee for better earnings
items.summary: Russian crude exports on G7 tankers fell sharply in October as Greek operators were enticed by strong earnings elsewhere and steered away from Black Sea conflicts, according to S&P Global Commodities at Sea(opens in a new tab) and Maritime Intelligence Risk Suite data. The data shows tankers flagged, owned or operated by companies based in G7 countries and their allies, or insured by Western protection and indemnity clubs, loaded roughly 906,000 barrels per day of Russian crude in October, or 24.2% of total exports. The share was the lowest in seven months. In September, G7 tankers lifted 1.2 million b/d, or 29.2% of total exports. October’s average Suezmax time-charter-equivalent earnings for transporting Russian crude from the Baltic to West Coast India was $46,257.92 per day lower than the Global Suezmax Index, compared with a discount of $23,225.69/day in September, according to Platts assessments for non-scrubber, non-eco ships. Greek tanker firms have also been avoiding operations in the Black Sea, with the CAS/MIRS data showing only one Greek-operated tanker lifting Russian crude in the region last month, compared with 11 in other regions. Platts assessed the additional war risk premium for crude exports from the Black Sea at $5/b on Nov.

items.title: Korea shipbuilders face LNG carrier price squeeze as North America orders seen next year
items.original_title: Korea shipbuilders face LNG carrier price squeeze as North America orders seen next year
items.summary: LNG carriers are the flagship high-margin vessel type where Korean shipbuilders have shown strength. According to Clarksons Research, the ship new building price for a 174,000-cubic-meter LNG carrier fell from an average of $248 million in January this year to $245 million in October. In fact, contract prices for newbuild LNG carriers at Samsung Heavy Industries, which has the most LNG carrier orders among Korean shipbuilders, have dropped from late last year and early this year. At its third-quarter earnings briefing on the 29th of last month, Samsung Heavy Industries acknowledged it had recently taken LNG carrier orders at low prices. Some analysts say China’s rising share of LNG carrier orders is pressuring Korean shipbuilders to lower prices. On the decline in Korea’s market share and prices due to China’s rising LNG carrier orders, Samsung Heavy Industries said it is “carefully monitoring developments in China.” Bae Gi-yeon, an analyst at Meritz Securities, said, “Capacity expansion and new entrants at Chinese shipyards are putting downward pressure on the ship new building price for LNG carriers,” adding, “The pricing competitiveness of low-cost LNG carriers from Chinese shipyards is bound to stand out.” The broader base of Chinese yards is forcing Korean shipbuilders to cut prices to win orders.

items.original_title: Carriers may secure only part of their November rate increases as Suez returns, Sogese report says
items.summary: Freight rates to Europe have rebounded since early October after falling steadily from their July peak, but the conditions behind the rebound are mixed. Cargo demand is positive, with Far East to Europe volumes up 12.2% in the first seven months of the year, according to Xeneta. Ships, however, are arriving late, and the return of Suez routings is releasing capacity faster than schedules are recovering. In its November Europe Container Market Update, Sogese reads this as a market moving from a disruption premium to a capacity-management test, in which the price carriers announce and the price shippers actually pay are drifting apart. If Suez keeps normalising, the key question for 2027 will not be whether there are enough ships, but how aggressively carriers manage the capacity that comes back into the market.”Andrea Monti, CEO & MD, Sogese 2. For its November outlook the report also sets out three paths: partial uptake of announced increases, failure of the increases to reach market rates, and uneven capacity and pricing as Suez rotations are rebuilt. Treat Drewry’s 12 and 19 November releases and the expiry of the 1 to 14 November FAKs as the first evidence of what the market will pay.

International Longshore and Warehouse Union (ILWU) Local 26, the union representing about 250 port watchmen at the ports of LA/LB, and the Pacific Maritime Association (PMA), which represents employers, will continue negotiating a new contract during the extension. Should the watchmen strike, operations at eight terminals in the port complex could be brought to a halt. Watchmen make up only 2% of ILWU workers at the two ports but work at terminals handling roughly 85% of Long Beach’s cargo and 33% of Los Angeles’ cargo. It is the third extension after the watchmen originally planned to strike on 4 November. Negotiations will continue with the assistance of the Federal Mediation and Conciliation Service (FMCS), PMA said in a statement on its website. The watchmen are not part of the agreement reached in 2023 between 29 West Coast ports and 22,000 workers that expires in 2028. Titanium dioxide (TiO2) is also shipped in containers. items.title: U.S. Formalizes Two-Month Extension of China Ship Port Fee Suspension
items.original_title: U.S. Formalizes Two-Month Extension of China Ship Port Fee Suspension
items.summary: The Trump administration has formally extended its suspension of port fees targeting Chinese-built and Chinese-operated vessels for another two months, keeping the controversial measures on hold while Washington continues trade negotiations with Beijing. The decision, published Tuesday in the Federal Register, extends the suspension through 11:59 p.m. Eastern Time on January 9, 2027, with the measures potentially resuming January 10 unless further action is taken. The extension took effect November 9, preventing the fees from returning following the expiration of an earlier one-year suspension agreed to under a trade deal between President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping in November 2025. The extension also maintains the suspension of additional duties on Chinese ship-to-shore cranes and other cargo-handling equipment. USTR said it will continue monitoring China’s maritime and shipbuilding practices and consider whether to extend the suspension again or take further action before the January 10 deadline. The decision comes as China has also extended its suspension of retaliatory port fees targeting U.S.-linked vessels until January 10, 2027, according to a Reuters report on Monday. China also extended its suspension of an investigation into the security of shipping and shipbuilding supply chains.

items.title: ‘Nonsense Rate’: Iran War Exposes Turmoil Behind Key Tanker Benchmark
items.original_title: ‘Nonsense Rate’: Iran War Exposes Turmoil Behind Key Tanker Benchmark
items.summary: By Jack Farchy and Alex Longley (Bloomberg) — In March this year, inside a 282-year-old institution responsible for one of the most important prices in global oil markets, one man staged a quiet protest. “Nonsense rate,” Christopher Loveday wrote on March 23 in an internal document at the Baltic Exchange, where he was responsible for helping produce the world’s benchmark rate for shipping oil. “Still a nonsense,” he wrote two days later. Collectively, they offer unprecedented insight into how the war in Iran played out inside a key corner of the global oil market. It has shown that numerous people involved in the key oil tanker rate, called TD3C, expressed reservations as the Baltic Exchange continued to publish the price in the early weeks of the war. Still, there were hopes that the war may end quickly, and when the Baltic held a call for its panelist brokers on March 4, the conclusion was that they were willing to keep submitting assessments. Still, he also said in court that he had thought since the start of the war that TD3C should have been suspended.

items.original_title: Hapag-Lloyd and Inmarsat Maritime: a case study in connected shipping
items.summary: Hapag-Lloyd, the world’s fifth-largest container carrier, operates 300 vessels on 133 liner services, transporting 13.5 million twenty-foot-equivalent units a year between 600 ports worldwide. Given the scale and complexity of these operations, every decision affects thousands of containers per vessel – with the consequences of any misstep felt throughout the supply chain. The company’s proactive approach to fleetwide digitalisation has therefore been devised with one overarching objective in mind: to simplify its operations. “We digitalise because there’s a use case for it – because there’s value we can drive.” For Hapag-Lloyd, tangible targets include maintaining schedule reliability above 90% across its network, reducing emissions per TEU by 30% by 2030, and approaching net-zero emissions by 2045 – all while cutting operating costs by approximately $100 per TEU. In this way, Briest explained, Hapag-Lloyd could keep commercial and environmental impacts to a minimum without compromising voyage safety. Digitalisation and connectivity, then, enable shipping companies like Hapag-Lloyd to make smarter operational decisions based on a richer and more immediate view of what is happening on the vessel and across the network. In a further operational scenario from the notional voyage, Briest explained that the Hapag-Lloyd LIVE tool allows customers to monitor refrigerated cargo and respond when circumstances change.

items.original_title: ‘Severe supply imbalance’ threat as record box ship deliveries loom
items.summary: The global containership fleet is set to expand by almost 50% by 2030, with even record levels of vessel scrapping unlikely to prevent a severe supply imbalance. In its latest report, Sea-Intelligence forecast the fleet will grow from almost 34m teu today to 40m teu by Q2 28, and 50m teu by the Q3 30. The analyst expects average annual fleet growth of 10% between 2027 and 2030, based on existing orders, with further newbuilding contracts potentially increasing that figure. Quarterly deliveries are forecast to average 1m teu over the period, peaking at 1.8m teu in the third quarter of 2028. This compares with average quarterly deliveries of 560,000 teu between 2023 and 2026, highlighting the scale of capacity due to enter the market. In 2016, carriers scrapped a record 670,000 teu, equivalent to just 3.3% of the fleet, during the industry’s previous overcapacity crisis. Jonathan Roach, analyst at Braemar, told The Loadstar there were 1,944 vessels aged 20 years or more, with 1,903 ships on order. Jan Tiedemann, VP liner strategy at Alphaliner, told The Loadstar he expected scrapping to increase in 2027 and 2028 without offsetting the newbuilding influx. He also pointed to the replacement needs of larger vessels built between 2000 and 2010, many of which will approach the end of their commercial lives in the mid-2030s.

The trade body identified approximately £123bn ($165.5bn) of potential UK offshore energy capital investment between 2026 and 2035 but warned that many projects remain uncertain. According to the report, 95% of companies surveyed believe they could expand capacity if domestic offshore activity increased. OEUK warned that offshore wind, carbon capture, and other emerging energy markets have not yet generated sufficient activity to replace traditional oil and gas work at scale. Katy Heidenreich, OEUK’s supply chain and people director, called for continued investment in domestic oil and gas alongside renewable energy developments. OEUK cautioned that losing specialist offshore capabilities now could leave the UK increasingly dependent on overseas suppliers when future energy projects move into construction.

items.summary: Oslo-listed Pelagic Credit has made its first move into the crude tanker sector, committing $30m in mezzanine financing for two suezmax vessels backed by charter employment with a Geneva-based commodities trading group. The Limassol-headquartered shipping investment company has agreed to provide an 18-month loan facility, which is expected to generate approximately $3m in distributable earnings from interest and fees over the financing period. The two tankers, each capable of transporting approximately 1m barrels of crude oil, will be employed on time charters with an unnamed independent global energy and commodities trader headquartered in Switzerland. The charters will run for the duration of the financing, providing contracted cash flows to support debt servicing. The identities of the vessels, their owner and the financing counterparty have not been disclosed. Pelagic Credit said the facility is backed by a security and corporate support package, with closing expected during November, subject to customary conditions. Chief executive Tobias Backer said the transaction marked another third-party investment for the company, extending its portfolio into the suezmax segment while maintaining its focus on contracted earnings.

items.summary: What do the numbers tell us about the global container shipping market in Q3 2026? We also explore the growing impact of port congestion, as typhoons and operational disruption put further pressure on already stretched supply chains, plus the contrasting developments in the Middle East with increasing returns to Red Sea transits and continued uncertainty around the Strait of Hormuz. Finally, we revisit the predictions made in our Q2 episode to see how they measured up, before asking Nigel and Gavin to look ahead and share their forecasts for the coming months. items.title: South Korea clears Sinar Mas takeover of Hyundai LNG Shipping
items.original_title: South Korea clears Sinar Mas takeover of Hyundai LNG Shipping
items.summary: South Korea has given conditional approval for the sale of Hyundai LNG Shipping to Indonesia’s Sinar Mas Group, removing the final regulatory hurdle in a deal that has been held up for months by national energy security concerns. The Ministry of Trade, Industry and Energy has completed a foreign investment security review, approving the transaction subject to undisclosed national security conditions. The sellers, a consortium comprising IMM Private Equity and IMM Investment, are now targeting November 23 to complete the transaction, nearly a year after signing a sale agreement with Sinar Mas. Hyundai LNG Shipping operates 12 LNG carriers and six LPG carriers and holds long-term transportation contracts with state-owned Korea Gas Corporation (KOGAS). The proposed foreign takeover has faced fierce opposition from South Korean shipowners, who warned that transferring control of strategically important gas carriers overseas could undermine national energy security and lead to the loss of maritime expertise. Sinar Mas has sought to address these concerns by pledging to maintain Korean-flag operations and protect existing employment. Hyundai LNG Shipping was carved out of Hyundai Merchant Marine, now HMM, in 2014. An attempt to sell the business back to HMM in 2023 collapsed over differences in valuation. The latest approval clears the way for IMM to exit its investment after 12 years.

items.title: LNG Bunker Snapshot: European LNG prices slump $235/mt on Middle East peace hopes
items.original_title: LNG Bunker Snapshot: European LNG prices slump $235/mt on Middle East peace hopes
items.summary: Rotterdam’s LNG bunker price has fallen by more than TTF, as its bunker premium has narrowed. Front-month TTF has fallen by $4.08/MMBtu ($212/mt) to $28.77/MMBtu ($1,496/mt). Rotterdam’s bunker premium over TTF has gone from $3.17/MMBtu ($165/mt) a week ago to $2.73/MMBtu ($142/mt), and the Baltic premium from $5.15/MMBtu ($268/mt) to $4.71/MMBtu ($245/mt). TTF fell sharply on 2 November after US President Donald Trump took a cautious stance on resuming military strikes against Iran, and slid further, as the US midterm election results fuelled hopes that the Middle East war could end soon, the Japan Organization for Metals and Energy Security (JOGMEC) said. Singapore’s LNG bunker price has fallen by nearly twice as much as JKM, but by less than the ARA’s, widening its premium over ARA from $13/mt a week ago to $109/mt. It rebounded on 6 November as uncertainty over the region persisted and supply stayed tight. In other LNG bunker news, US floating LNG infrastructure company Excelerate Energy will supply up to around 307,000 mt/year of LNG for 11 years to AxDo Bahamas, a small-scale LNG and bunker venture formed by LNG bunker supplier Axpo and Bahamas-based Domicisle LNG, with the first deliveries expected next year.

items.title: Shipbroker’s document delay leads to US$24,000 demurrage settlement, ITIC warns
items.original_title: Shipbroker’s document delay leads to US$24,000 demurrage settlement, ITIC warns
items.summary: A shipbroker contributed US$24,000 towards a settlement of a demurrage dispute after delays in forwarding key documents complicated a claim between shipowners and charterers, according to a case highlighted by International Transport Intermediaries Club (ITIC) in its most recent Claims Review. The dispute concerned a demurrage claim, valued at approximately US$48,000, which the owners were pursuing against charterers for delays at discharge. The shipbroker became involved after failing to pass on supporting documents relating to the claim. However, the broker’s delay in forwarding key documents meant the charterers’ objections did not reach the owners promptly, reducing the opportunity to address any deficiencies in the claim. Given the weaknesses in the underlying demurrage claim, the matter was settled with the shipbroker contributing US$24,000, half the value of the claim, towards the owners’ losses. “In this case, the delay reduced the owners’ chance to deal with problems in their claim early. Expert support in assessing liability and negotiating a resolution can make a real difference to the result. Demurrage claims often carry tight contractual time bars, so claims and supporting documents should be passed on as soon as they arrive, with a record of when that happened. Even a short delay can prejudice a party’s position and prove costly.” Source: International Transport Intermediaries Club (ITIC)

items.title: China Overtakes Korea LNG Carrier Orders, Challenging Korea’s Market Lead
items.original_title: China Overtakes Korea LNG Carrier Orders, Challenging Korea’s Market Lead
items.summary: South Korea’s long-standing lead in the global market for large liquefied natural gas (LNG) carriers is facing growing competition. China secured more LNG carrier orders than Korea in October, challenging its position in the high-value shipbuilding segment. According to Clarkson Research, a British shipbuilding and shipping market research firm, China secured five of the seven large LNG carriers ordered worldwide in October, while Korea won the remaining two. Korea retained the lead with 44 vessels, or 57.9% of the total, while China secured 32, accounting for 42.1%. China, which received just three LNG carrier orders in all of 2025, has already secured more than 10 times that number this year. Jiangnan has likewise secured a series of overseas orders, including two 175,000-cubic-meter LNG carriers from Singapore-based Eastern Pacific Shipping (EPS) earlier this year and four vessels from ADNOC Logistics & Services, the shipping subsidiary of the UAE’s state-owned energy company. China secured 61.03 million CGT, accounting for 76.6% of the total, while Korea received 11.91 million CGT, or 14.9%. During the same period last year, China held a 63.3% share and Korea 16.4%.

items.title: G7 Launches Global Port Security Network to Combat Drug Trafficking
items.original_title: G7 Launches Global Port Security Network to Combat Drug Trafficking
items.summary: France on Monday laurched a new G7-backed network linking major seaports, customs authorities and international organizations in an effort to crack down on drug trafficking through global maritime supply chains. The G7+ Ports Network to Combat Drug Trafficking, announced during the G7 foreign ministers’ meeting in Paris on November 9, brings together 14 ports and participating countries, including Brazil and South Korea, alongside the G7 nations. The initiative aims to improve intelligence sharing, strengthen cooperation between port and customs authorities, and better identify shipping routes and containers being exploited by criminal organizations. The network was first proposed at the G7 leaders’ summit in Évian, France, in June, when leaders issued a joint declaration identifying maritime transport as the primary route for international drug and precursor chemical trafficking. According to France’s Foreign Ministry , the network is holding its first meeting in Marseille alongside the November 9–10 G7 ministerial gathering in Paris. In their June declaration, G7 leaders warned that criminal organizations increasingly rely on access to legitimate public and private institutions to facilitate international drug shipments. They also called for stronger cooperation with the private sector and improvements to port and shipping security standards.

items.title: IMO Warns of Mounting Human Toll as Attacks on Commercial Shipping Continue
items.original_title: IMO Warns of Mounting Human Toll as Attacks on Commercial Shipping Continue
items.summary: A sailor observes the oil tanker HELGA, which is moored at one of Iraq's southern offshore oil terminals near Basra, as it prepares to load crude oil, April 24, 2026. REUTERS/Mohammed Aty The International Maritime Organization (IMO) is calling for stronger protections for merchant ships and their crews as continued attacks in the Middle East, Red Sea and Black Sea put seafarers at risk and threaten vital shipping routes. The warning follows the IMO Council’s 138th session in London last week, where members addressed a growing list of maritime security threats, including the war involving Iran, Houthi attacks in the Red Sea and Russian strikes on shipping and port infrastructure in Ukraine. “Seafarers continue to lose their lives, suffer serious injuries, face abandonment, are denied repatriation and are deprived of basic human necessities, including water, food and medical care, resulting from the ongoing geopolitical conflicts,” IMO Secretary-General Arsenio Dominguez said. The Council strongly condemned Houthi attacks against merchant vessels and crews in the Red Sea and Bab al-Mandab Strait, as well as Russian attacks targeting commercial ships, seafarers, ports and maritime safety infrastructure supporting Ukraine’s Black Sea shipping corridor. The Council also selected China’s Yu Jiajia as the recipient of the 2027 IMO Gender Equality Award.

Spot prices for mainstream products at Qingdao Port fell by an average of about 3 yuan/mt. Trader activity was moderate, steel mill inquiries were limited, and overall spot transactions were thin. 6, iron ore inventory at 35 major ports nationwide stood at 149.13 million mt, up 1.08 million mt WoW. Arrivals are expected to rebound next week, and port inventory may accumulate further. Hot metal production at steel mill blast furnaces pulled back, and port cargo pick-up weakened in tandem. Overall, the rebound momentum driven by bear position liquidation has faded somewhat, and with port inventory buildup pressure persisting, the upside in futures is capped. In the short term, iron ore prices may shift to consolidating at highs, a downgrade from yesterday’s slightly bullish view. items.title: Iran: US strikes ship after Hormuz blockade breach
items.original_title: Iran: US strikes ship after Hormuz blockade breach
items.summary: The United States struck a commercial ship attempting to breach its naval blockade on Iran, the US military said. According to the US Central Command (CENTCOM), the cargo vessel “tried to depart regional waters after visiting an Iranian port,” before its stern was struck by “precision munitions” shot from a US military aircraft. In a video posted by CENTCOM, an explosion can be seen on the M/V Huda’s stern as a result of the shooting, with the ship’s civilian crew ignoring “repeated warnings.” The authorities in the UAE said 22 people had been rescued due to a fire on a vessel in the Gulf of Oman. The US naval blockade on Iran, intended to pressure the country into lifting its own blockade on the Strait of Hormuz, has been in force for months. Iran’s own blockade of the waterway, through which a fifth of the world’s oil and gas supplies flowed before the war started in late February, saw energy prices spike around the world. Tehran has regularly attacked vessels going through the Strait of Hormuz without its approval. Aramco building hit after rocket attack Elsewhere in the Middle East, the escalation between Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen and Saudi Arabia continued to rage.

items.title: HMM Platinum general average adds to cargo woes, as search for refuge drags on
items.original_title: HMM Platinum general average adds to cargo woes, as search for refuge drags on
items.summary: HMM has declared general average following the fire aboard the HMM Platinum , generating a slew of new hurdles for cargo owners, with the carrier still seeking a port of refuge for the vessel, which has spent the past month anchored off the South African coast. Korhi Average Adjusters & Surveyors have been appointed to handle the adjustment for the 5,593 teu containership, with Korhi and Richards Hogg Lindley responsible for collecting general average security. Those with cargo aboard will be required to provide salvage security and general average security before shipments can be forwarded or released, while uninsured cargo owners will be required to provide cash deposits, although the amounts have yet to be determined. Given the extent of cargo damage and timetable for discharging containers remains unclear, the requirements add more uncertainty for forwarders and their customers with shipments aboard the vessel. Fire broke out aboard the Liberian-flagged vessel on 6 October, while sailing from Kattupalli to Santos, with reports claiming that the blaze originated in a container while the ship was off Madagascar’s southern coast, with some 2,300 boxes aboard. Salvage specialist SMIT was appointed under a Lloyd’s Open Form agreement, while the vessel diverted towards South Africa but finding a suitable port of refuge has proved complicated.

items.original_title: COSCO unveils massive supertanker fleet push
items.summary: Chinese tanker giant COSCO Shipping Energy Transportation has unveiled a sweeping fleet expansion involving 24 VLCC newbuildings, signing contracts worth RMB9.48bn ($1.42bn) for ten supertankers and lining up another 14 through long-term bareboat charters. The Shanghai- and Hong Kong-listed owner disclosed the deals on November 9, with its wholly owned subsidiary Hainan Cosco Shipping Energy Transportation placing orders at two Chinese shipyards. Six VLCCs have been contracted at Yangzhou COSCO Shipping Heavy Industry for RMB5.69bn ($853m), while Dalian Shipbuilding Industry Corporation (DSIC) has secured four vessels worth RMB3.79bn ($569m). Alongside the direct newbuilding investment, COSCO Shipping Energy has approved plans to take another 14 VLCC newbuildings on bareboat charter from six Chinese financial leasing companies. Taken together, the announcements cover ten directly ordered VLCCs and another 14 planned chartered newbuildings, marking a major expansion of Cosco Shipping Energy’s crude tanker fleet heading into the next decade. The company said further information would be disclosed once specific agreements are signed, leaving it unclear whether the 16 vessels represent additional fleet expansion or overlap with other newbuilding plans. The proposed charters will run for up to 20 years, with the ships scheduled to enter the fleet during 2030.The largest allocation is four LNG dual-fuel VLCCs from Bank of Communications Financial Leasing, carrying a maximum combined rental commitment of RMB5.2bn ($779m).

The latest deal extends an aggressive fleet expansion programme that has seen RCL return repeatedly to Chinese shipbuilders while also moving into larger vessel classes. In September, the carrier signed for four 3,100 teu ships at CSSC Huangpu Wenchong, taking its programme at the Guangzhou yard to 16 vessels across three designs. That deal followed an order for four 1,900 teu feeders in August. RCL also turned to South Korea’s HD Hyundai Heavy Industries last November for two 14,000 teu ships in a KRW435.3bn ($299m) contract, marking its first newbuilding agreement with the yard.

items.title: ‘Multi-node supply chains’ are the future, in a ‘multi-polar pharma world’
items.original_title: ‘Multi-node supply chains’ are the future, in a ‘multi-polar pharma world’
items.summary: China, India, and the Middle East are all playing their role in shifting the geographical centre of production and innovation, the three regions emerging as particularly important to the global pharmaceutical supply chain Frank van Gelder, secretary general of Pharma.Aero, said a fracturing of the supply chain with a more geographically diffuse network of production, healthcare providers, and clinical centres could create new opportunities for airfreight and specialist logistics providers. “China is no longer only a major source of pharmaceutical ingredients and manufacturing capacity; it is becoming an increasingly important centre for biotechnology, clinical development, and innovative medicines,” he told The Loadstar . “India remains essential to generics and manufacturing, while expanding its innovative capabilities; Europe and North America remain central, but innovation and production are becoming more geographically distributed. While Europe and North America would remain important pharma centres, he said the emergence of additional innovation and production hubs was creating what he called a “multi-polar pharmaceutical world”. For logistics providers, “that means multi-node supply chains – interconnected manufacturing sites, clinical centres, specialised logistics hubs, and healthcare delivery points, rather than dependence on a few dominant origins and gateways”, Mr van Gelder explained.

items.title: Cargo boycott threat by Indian brokers over empty-box fee hikes
items.original_title: Cargo boycott threat by Indian brokers over empty-box fee hikes
items.summary: A new storm of stakeholder disputes, and potential operational disruption, is brewing across Indian ports over policy changes by container lines on empty-container handling and associated depot charges. The loading and unloading of empty boxes at yards is the flashpoint for discontent and disagreement between supply chain intermediaries and carriers. Maersk, for example, has substantially raised its lift-on/lift-off (lo-lo) charges for empties moving via Mundra, India’s busiest container port and the primary gateway for the hinterlands around Delhi. The revision, implemented from 1 November, effectively more than doubled the rates shippers had been charged, from $23 to $51 per 20ft empty box, and from $31 to $67 per 40ft, plus local taxes. Ondeed, one liner source told The Loadstar : “We are discussing the matter.” At Chennai, MSC seems to be facing the brunt of a trade pushback against the practice of routing empty tariff collections through third-party depot vendors, which cargo agents claim opens the market to an unregulated environment. “MSC has taken the lead in implementing this collection practice in Chennai, following which other shipping lines have initiated similar measures,” the Chennai Customs Brokers Association (CCBA) noted. The CCBA claimed the policy shift was fraught with “serious economic and operational implications for cargo agents”, as it had seen third-party vendors keep inflating tariffs once taken over.

items.title: India’s coking coal import dependence on Australia falls to 54%
items.original_title: India’s coking coal import dependence on Australia falls to 54%
items.summary: India’s dependence on Australia for coking coal imports fell to 54% in 2025 from 73% in 2019, according to a deposition by the steel ministry to a parliamentary standing committee. About 90% of India’s coking coal requirement, a key raw material for steelmaking via the BF-BOF route, is met through imports because India has limited availability of high-quality, low-ash coking coal. Australia remains India’s largest source of coking coal imports, but the share of Russia rose from 0.62% to 8.15%, the US from 8% to 17%, Mozambique from 4% to 7.31% and Indonesia from 2.46% to 4%. India’s steel sector imported 58 Mt of coking coal in FY25, up from 57 Mt in FY24, at a cost of around Rs 1.5 lakh crore. Under the Aatmanirbhar Coal Mission, the government’s Mission Coking Coal targets 140 Mt of domestic raw coking coal production by 2030 – 105 Mt from Coal India Limited and 35 Mt from private allocations – while aiming to raise the blending ratio of domestic coal in steelmaking from 10% to 30%. Globally, high-quality hard coking coal is concentrated in a few countries, and Australia accounts for more than 50% of internationally traded coking coal owing to its high-quality reserves, stable mining ecosystem and efficient logistics. Source: SMM

items.summary: Black Sea flows remain minimal The Black Sea picture is stark. Vessels sit at anchor offshore, waiting to enter the Danube to load, and the backlog is large. Ukrainian shipments from Izmail and Reni are vital for the export campaign, though volumes are relatively low. Baltic EU grain is moving to Sub-Saharan Africa, and French wheat is winning more North African business. The latest World Agricultural Supply and Demand Estimates (WASDE) cut 25 million bushels from the US export campaign, and a couple of Polish wheat shipments have reached the US. Australia is near 30 Mt despite El Niño, and Argentina is at 21 to 22 Mt, relatively large compared to the past five to 10 years. Panamaxes now carry around 60% of Australian coal, which competes with grain cargoes and lifts rates. There are close to 260 Panamax ballasters in the Indian Ocean, against 170 a year ago and a five-year average of about 160. Close to 150 ballasting Supramaxes are in the Black Sea and Mediterranean region, ahead of last year.

items.title: LNG Shipping Market Posts Weekly Gains
items.original_title: LNG Shipping Market Posts Weekly Gains
items.summary: The LNG market strengthened this week, with relatively high fixing activity east of Suez helping to tighten vessel availability. The Atlantic also saw a gradual improvement in spot rates, although cargo demand remains relatively subdued and the tonnage list continues to limit further upside. On the BLNG1 Australia–Japan route, rates increased by $9,600 week-on-week to settle at $54,600/day. The six-month rate increased by $1,700 to $44,200/day, while the one-year term rose by $200 to $54,067/day. Further out the curve, the three-year period edged lower by $100 to $70,500/day. The LPG market firmed this week, with a healthy level of fixture activity in the West supporting rates. On the BLPG1 Ras Tanura–Chiba route, rates settled at $261.40 per tonne, with TCE earnings closing at $254,022/day. The BLPG2 Houston–Flushing route increased by $5.33 week-on-week to settle at $180.00 per tonne, with TCE earnings rising by $9,610 to $210,924/day. Similarly, the BLPG3 Houston–Chiba route gained $8.29 to close at $322.29 per tonne, while TCE returns increased by $10,491 to $196,055/day.

items.title: IMO faces calls to enhance maritime security code amid rising threats
items.original_title: IMO faces calls to enhance maritime security code amid rising threats
items.summary: The International Association of Ports and Harbors has called on the International Maritime Organization to update the world’s main maritime security regulatory framework, as escalating attacks on commercial shipping and emerging cyber and technology risks expose potential gaps in rules largely unchanged for more than two decades. In a statement Nov. 5, the industry group representing roughly 400 ports and related businesses globally said there was a case for updated guidance around the International Ship and Port Facility Security Code to reflect modern port operations and strengthen cooperation between governments and industry. The debate comes amid severe disruption to key energy shipping routes amid persistent security concerns. Jeremy Greenwood, head of the IMO’s Maritime Security Section, welcomed further discussion on the ISPS code but stressed that increasing threats did not necessarily mean the regulation itself was fundamentally flawed. Adopted in 2002 and mandatory since 2004 under the International Convention for the Safety of Life at Sea, the ISPS Code sets security requirements for ships and ports, covering access controls, threat assessments, security plans and operational procedures. Code revamp A US proposal this year said the code had not undergone a significant revision since adoption despite evolving security threats to merchant shipping. The IMO is due to hold the next meeting of the Maritime Safety Committee during Dec.
