items.summary: Xeneta, the AI-powered ocean and air freight intelligence solution, today announced its largest set of product launches at the 10th annual Xeneta Summit, Munich. Presented live to over 600 shippers, forwarders and carriers, the launches mark a shift in what Xeneta does for its customers. For 14 years, Xeneta has given freight procurement the data to see the market; now it moves into the decisions that data informs and the actions that follow. The launches span three areas: new data, led by the first dataset to show both the announced and the actual transit time of cargo moving via a transshipment hub and an air benchmark covering over 17M tonnes of airfreight on 92% more lanes than before; AI Agents with embedded Xeneta freight expertise reading a customer’s contracts against the market and recommending what to do first; and new execution tools, Xeneta Rate Management (XRM) and Xeneta Tender, that put the live market rate next to every contract and every bid, so teams manage rates and award tenders on evidence they can defend. The new Xeneta Transshipment dataset shows how long shipments really take on indirect routes, by carrier and by hub, promised against actual, taking Xeneta total ocean coverage to 27,000 lanes.

items.original_title: A.E. Nomikos adds Oshima kamsarmax to fleet renewal drive
items.summary: Greek dry bulk owner A.E. Nomikos Shipping Investments has returned to Japan’s Oshima Shipbuilding for a kamsarmax newbuilding, continuing its fleet renewal programme with a vessel scheduled to join its fleet towards the end of the decade. The Piraeus-based company confirmed the contract was signed with Sumisho Marine involved in the deal. Shipbroking sources have placed delivery in 2029, although the owner’s website lists the vessel for 2030. The 82,000 dwt newbuilding, provisionally named Leontari SB , has already been added to the company’s fleet register. Nomikos said the order marked another step in its efforts to renew and expand its fleet, maintaining its long-standing focus on Japanese-built tonnage. Established in 1985, the Greek company currently operates four bulk carriers, including the 2009-built, 82,553 dwt Astraea SB, also constructed at Oshima. Its remaining fleet comprises three smaller bulkers built by Japan Marine United between 2014 and 2015: the 60,990 dwt sisterships Filosofia SB and Attiki SB, and the 55,685 dwt Alkyoni SB. The latest investment will bring another kamsarmax into the fleet, strengthening Nomikos’s presence in the segment while adding younger tonnage to its Japanese-built portfolio.

items.title: Boluda buys Dutch offshore towage specialist
items.original_title: Boluda buys Dutch offshore towage specialist
items.summary: Spanish towage giant Boluda has acquired Dutch offshore towage and heavy transport specialist Muller Dordrecht, adding 16 tugs and eight barges to its growing global fleet. The takeover gives Boluda full ownership of the century-old family business, whose fleet includes seven offshore tugs specialising in complex marine transportation, rig moves, anchor handling and offshore wind projects. Financial terms of the transaction have not been disclosed. Muller, founded in 1918 and headquartered in Dordrecht, will continue operating as an independent unit under the name Boluda Muller Towage, retaining its existing management team and focusing on offshore towage and marine projects worldwide. The Dutch operator has built a sizeable presence in the North Sea and Baltic markets, supporting offshore energy and infrastructure projects ranging from transporting wind turbine foundations and offshore substations to heavy lifting and coastal towage. Its fleet includes the 120-tonne bollard pull En Avant 30 and the 90-tonne bollard pull En Avant 25 and En Avant 26 , which can operate both offshore and in ports. Boluda Towage executive chairman Vicente Boluda Ceballos said the acquisition would broaden the group’s specialist offshore capabilities while allowing Muller to continue developing its operations alongside Boluda’s existing European business.

items.original_title: Russia Takes Control of Two Chinese Heavy-Lift Ships Used for Arctic LNG 2 Deliveries
items.summary: Glory Ocean with 3-TMR-001 module on board off the coast of Singapore on May 5. (Source: Supplied) Russia has taken control of two modern heavy-lift carriers previously involved in transporting equipment for the sanctioned Arctic LNG 2 project , adding specialized project cargo vessels to an expanding network of shipping assets supporting the country’s Arctic energy ambitions. The ownership change gives Moscow greater control over a critical part of the supply chain for its Arctic energy projects, from transporting construction modules to remote project sites to potentially delivering finished LNG infrastructure to future overseas customers. The two vessels have a history of transporting oversized equipment for Arctic LNG 2. The subsequent voyage to Arctic LNG 2 was conducted largely outside public tracking. They eventually delivered the modules to the Utrenniy terminal serving Arctic LNG 2 without broadcasting their positions. At least seven additional modules intended for Arctic LNG 2’s third train remain in China, according to satellite imagery, with some appearing complete and others still under construction. The development comes as two other Chinese heavy-lift carriers with connections to Russian Arctic shipping have attracted attention off Norway’s northern coast near Andøya . One of them, Ya Qing Hai Yang , formerly known as Ocean 28 , delivered a substation module from China to Arctic LNG 2 in 2024.

items.title: Record supply growth pushes container fleet towards 50m teu by 2030
items.original_title: Record supply growth pushes container fleet towards 50m teu by 2030
items.summary: The global containership fleet is heading towards an unprecedented 50m teu by 2030, setting the stage for a potentially devastating oversupply crisis and enormous downward pressure on freight rates. New analysis from Sea-Intelligence shows the fleet expanding from today’s 34m teu to 40m teu by the second quarter of 2028 and 50m teu by the third quarter of 2030, the largest capacity expansion in container shipping history. Combined with an estimated 8% effective capacity boost from the return of Asia-Europe services to the Suez Canal, cumulative supply growth could exceed 50% by the end of the decade. The consultancy calculates that quarterly newbuilding deliveries will average 1m teu between 2027 and 2030, peaking at an extraordinary 1.8m teu in the third quarter of 2028. Even if carriers repeated the record demolition levels of 2016 every year through 2030, this would absorb less than 17% of incoming capacity, leaving annual fleet growth averaging 8.5%. By 2030, some 10.8m teu will be aboard ships older than 20 years, although Sea-Intelligence doubts carriers intend to scrap anything approaching that figure. The warnings follow a similarly bearish forecast from Xeneta, which expects fleet growth of 6.8% next year against demand growth of just 2.5% to 4%.

items.title: Black Sea shipping reels from fresh attacks and record insurance costs
items.original_title: Black Sea shipping reels from fresh attacks and record insurance costs
items.summary: The Black Sea has experienced another violent weekend, with Russia claiming fresh strikes on merchant ships, human remains discovered aboard a damaged tanker in Bulgaria and war-risk insurance premiums reaching an extraordinary 20% of hull value. Russia’s defence ministry issued a succession of statements over the weekend claiming to have attacked commercial vessels carrying military supplies for Ukraine. On Saturday, Moscow reported hitting a dry cargo ship southeast of Odesa, followed by another claim involving a vessel east of the Ukrainian port. Romanian radar detected two aerial targets near Snake Island on Sunday, prompting Spanish F-18 fighters and NH90 helicopters to scramble from the Mihail Kogălniceanu airbase. Bulgaria, Romania and Turkey activated their joint Black Sea mine-countermeasures group on Saturday, with vessels participating in the Poseidon 2026 exercise off Bulgaria. The mounting attacks are producing unprecedented insurance costs. Black Sea war-risk insurance premiums have reached as much as 20% of vessel value for particularly exposed voyages, according to insurance market sources, exceeding even the extraordinary rates seen during the Iran-Iraq tanker war of the 1980s. For comparison, historical research from the University of Texas and contemporary reporting from the London insurance market show tanker-war premiums reaching 7.5% and occasionally exceeding 10% during the 1980s.

items.summary: Merchant shipping has been caught in an extraordinary escalation of the war around the Strait of Hormuz over the past 72 hours, with tankers set ablaze, the US military bombing a bulk carrier, fresh Iranian warnings about naval mines and explosions reported along Iran’s southern coastline. The most dramatic American action came on Saturday when a US military aircraft fired precision-guided munitions at the stern of the St Kitts and Nevis-flagged bulk carrier Huda in the Gulf of Oman. US Central Command (CENTCOM) said the 1999-built vessel had repeatedly ignored warnings while attempting to leave regional waters after visiting an Iranian port, in violation of Washington’s naval blockade. The first incident occurred at approximately 19.20 UTC, eight nautical miles northwest of Khasab, Oman, where a tanker caught fire and its crew was evacuated. Elsewhere, the UAE National Guard announced on Sunday that it had rescued 22 Arab seafarers from a burning cargo vessel in the Gulf of Oman. According to BRS Shipbrokers, 141 tankers are now dedicated to shuttling crude and products from Gulf terminals through Hormuz to the Gulf of Oman or India’s west coast, where cargoes are transferred onto other vessels. VLCCs account for 72% of these shuttlers.

items.title: Ravi Mehrotra returns to shipyards with $470m VLAC order
items.original_title: Ravi Mehrotra returns to shipyards with $470m VLAC order
items.summary: Ravi Mehrotra’s Foresight Group is returning to the newbuilding market after a decade-long absence, with the London-based shipowner linked to a $470m order for four very large ammonia carriers (VLACs) at South Korea’s HD Hyundai Heavy Industries. The 90,000 cu m vessels are scheduled for delivery across 2029 and 2030, according to shipbroking sources, marking the opening move in a broader fleet investment programme reportedly worth around $1.2bn. HD Hyundai confirmed the contract in a regulatory filing, putting its value at KRW630.1bn ($470m), or approximately $117.5m per vessel. The Korean shipbuilder identified the customer only as an Africa-based shipping company, but shipbroking sources have linked the deal to Mehrotra’s Foresight. The latest move marks a shift towards newbuilding investment for the group, which has expanded its gas carrier business largely through secondhand purchases in recent years. Foresight currently lists seven large LPG carriers in its fleet, including the Jagannath, Badrinath and Kedarnath, all built by Hyundai Heavy Industries. The group has set its sights on building a fleet of 25 modern VLGCs by 2034, positioning itself for further expansion in the LPG sector and emerging ammonia trades.

items.original_title: Leon Shipping makes dry bulk debut with Hengli order
items.summary: Greek shipowner Panos Efthimiadis is making his first move into dry bulk shipping, with his Leon Shipping & Trading linked to a kamsarmax newbuilding at China’s Hengli Heavy Industries as its orderbook grows to five vessels. The Athens-based company has also been linked to two LR1 product tanker newbuildings, adding to a pair of 50,000 dwt MR tankers recently booked at Cosco Shipping Heavy Industry (Guangdong). Details of the LR1 contracts, including the shipyard, delivery dates and pricing, have yet to emerge. Pricing has not been disclosed, although current market assessments put similar MR newbuildings at around $53m each, suggesting a combined benchmark of approximately $106m. Brokers have linked the 2008-built, 50,000 dwt Leon Wisdom to a $26m sale to Union Maritime, while sistership Leon Grace was sold last month for a reported $23.5m to UAE interests and subsequently renamed Bella Sky . Both vessels were acquired earlier this year from International Seaways for a combined $32m. The reported sales would therefore generate approximately $17.5m above their original purchase prices, before transaction and other costs. Efthimiadis established Leon Shipping & Trading in 2010 after spending 22 years with family-owned Lotus Shipping. The Hengli contract would mark its first investment in dry bulk tonnage, adding a new segment to its fleet renewal and expansion programme.

items.title: Russia Says It Hit Three Cargo Ships In Black Sea
items.original_title: Russia Says It Hit Three Cargo Ships In Black Sea
items.summary: A cargo vessel leaves a port in the Black Sea, amid Russia's attack on Ukraine, in Odesa, Ukraine March 26, 2025. REUTERS/Nina Liashonok MOSCOW, Nov 8 (Reuters) – Russia said on Sunday overnight strikes by its forces had hit three cargo vessels that were carrying military goods for Ukraine and two electricity substations, which it said supplied power to the Ukrainian defense industry. The Defence Ministry said Russian forces had struck a container ship delivering weapons and military equipment to the Black Sea port of Odesa, and another in the port of Chornomorsk, which is in the same southwestern region of Ukraine. It said a third vessel, a dry cargo ship hit south-west of Odesa, was carrying weapons and military equipment for Ukraine’s armed forces. The ministry also said Russia had hit two power substations in Ukraine’s Dnipropetrovsk and Zhytomyr regions, both of which it said powered military-industrial enterprises. Ukrainian power company DTEK said a Russian overnight attack on energy facilities in Dnipropetrovsk had left more than 600,000 people without electricity. After seven strikes on cargo ships near NATO members Romania and Bulgaria last month, the US-led military alliance said it would deploy maritime patrol aircraft, radars and drones to bolster its eastern flank in the Black Sea.

items.title: Banks step up pressure on Havila Shipping over $78m debt dispute
items.original_title: Banks step up pressure on Havila Shipping over $78m debt dispute
items.summary: Norwegian offshore vessel owner Havila Shipping is facing renewed enforcement action from three major banks seeking to establish security liens over the company’s assets in connection with a long-running debt restructuring dispute. DNB, Swedbank, and Danske Bank have submitted a new request for attachment liens covering NOK779m ($78m), comprising NOK713m in principal and approximately NOK65m in accrued interest. The latest move follows a ruling by Norway’s Borgarting Court of Appeal on October 19, which went against Havila in its dispute with the lenders over a restructuring agreement dating back to 2020. Havila has said it disagrees with the judgment and intends to appeal to the Norwegian Supreme Court. The deadline for filing the appeal is November 19. The dispute centres on whether Havila breached the restructuring agreement by refinancing debt owed to lenders that had opted for a cash settlement in December 2024. The three banks, which financed the offshore support vessels Havila Foresight and Havila Harmony , maintain that the refinancing violated the agreement and have since demanded repayment of the outstanding debt. Havila has disputed the lenders’ interpretation, arguing that the banks were obliged to convert certain non-interest-bearing debt tranches into shares under the restructuring arrangements.

items.title: Meyer Werft sets up offshore business to handle $2.8bn converter orderbook
items.original_title: Meyer Werft sets up offshore business to handle $2.8bn converter orderbook
items.summary: German shipbuilding group Meyer Werft is setting up a dedicated offshore business to manage its growing involvement in North Sea converter platform construction. The new company, Neptun Offshore, will bring together the group’s offshore converter activities and hold its 50% stake in Neptun Smulders Offshore Renewables (NSORe), a joint venture with Belgian steel construction specialist Smulders. NSORe secured two major offshore converter contracts from German transmission system operator 50Hertz earlier this year for the LanWin3 and LanWin6 grid connection projects in the North Sea. The joint venture’s share of the contracts is valued at approximately €2.5bn ($2.8bn), with a substantial proportion of the work expected to take place in the German state of Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, including at Neptun Werft’s facilities in Rostock. Both projects involve 2GW offshore converter platforms designed to transmit electricity generated by North Sea wind farms to the German power grid. Meyer Werft said the decision to establish a separate company reflects the different technical, regulatory and financial requirements of converter platform construction compared with conventional shipbuilding. Neptun Offshore will be a wholly owned subsidiary of Meyer Werft, headed by Malte Poelmann, who already serves as managing director of NSORe alongside Dieter Weyns. The group aims to have the new structure established ahead of the construction of the first converter platform in 2028.

items.title: IMO Council urges stronger protection of seafarers amid threats to global shipping
items.original_title: IMO Council urges stronger protection of seafarers amid threats to global shipping
items.summary: Council condemns attacks on merchant shipping in the Red Sea and Black Sea, mourns loss of 25th seafarer since onset of Strait of Hormuz conflict, and renews Secretary-General’s tenure. The Council of the International Maritime Organization (IMO) has reaffirmed its commitment to protecting the safety, security, health and well-being of seafarers amid continuing threats to international shipping. Meeting for its 138th session at IMO Headquarters in London (2–6 November 2026), the Council reiterated that vital shipping lanes should remain open, safe and secure. The Council called on Member States to refrain from unlawful measures that would jeopardize the safety of seafarers and international shipping. Other key decisions Renewal of the Secretary-General’s mandate The Council decided to renew the mandate of IMO Secretary-General Arsenio Domínguez for another four-year term, concluding on 31 December 2031, and to make a recommendation to the 35th regular session of the IMO Assembly, in accordance with Article 22 of the IMO Convention. 2027 IMO Gender Equality Award The Council decided to award the 2027 IMO Gender Equality Award to Ms. Funding approved for IMO digital platforms The Council approved the Secretary-General’s funding proposal to complete the upgrade of the IMO’s Global Integrated Shipping Information System (GISIS) and develop an e-Learning platform, in an initial amount of GBP 2 million.

items.title: Egypt’s October wheat imports nearly triple, corn imports fall 35%
items.original_title: Egypt’s October wheat imports nearly triple, corn imports fall 35%
items.summary: Egypt imported 985,425 metric tons of wheat in October 2026, according to local shipping data from LATT Trading & Shipping, nearly tripling September’s total but down 47% year over year. Russia regained its position as Egypt’s largest supplier in October, shipping 403,245 mt, up 272% month on month. Russian wheat exported from the Baltic became more prominent: Latvian ports supplied 107,819 mt and a Lithuanian port supplied 30,700 mt, accounting for 14% of October imports. Ukrainian wheat arrivals almost doubled to 269,070 mt from September, representing 27% of October imports. The fall in prices was also driven by the state’s sales of wheat to private mills at EGP 16,650/mt, lower than the ex-warehouse prices. Corn imports fall on currency fluctuations, sufficient stocks Egypt’s corn imports totaled 777,269 metric tons in October 2026, down 35% month over month and 42.2% year over year, according to local shipping data from LATT Trading & Shipping. Market participants consequently expect imports to slow further in November, with one importer estimating Brazilian arrivals at around 450,000 mt. Platts-assessed Ukrainian corn averaged $220.81/mt in October, down $3.59/mt from $224.40/mt in September. Platts-assessed Brazilian corn averaged $223.82/mt in October, down $16.67/mt from $240.49/mt in September, and Argentine corn averaged $216.70/mt in October, down $9.39/mt from $226.10/mt in September.

items.title: HPCL Struggles To Book Tankers For Hormuz Crude
items.original_title: HPCL Struggles To Book Tankers For Hormuz Crude
items.summary: Vessel shortages and last-minute withdrawals by shipowners complicate crude shipments from the Persian Gulf despite recovering regional supplies Hindustan Petroleum Corporation Ltd (HPCL) is facing difficulties securing tankers to transport crude from inside the Persian Gulf through the Strait of Hormuz, as vessel shortages and last-minute withdrawals by shipowners complicate shipment arrangements, according to media reports. The challenge persists even as crude supplies from the Middle East recover and more vessels resume crossings through the strategic waterway. HPCL Chairman Vikas Kaushal said in an interview in Abu Dhabi this week that finding ships for available loading dates remains difficult, with some shipowners withdrawing even after agreeing to transport cargoes. HPCL bought an average of about 2,40,000 barrels per day of Middle Eastern crude in 2025, according to data from energy intelligence provider Kpler. The volume declined to 57,000 barrels per day in April 2026, when the conflict severely disrupted shipping through the Strait of Hormuz. Purchases subsequently recovered to an average of 256,000 barrels per day in October as more supplies from the region became available, Kpler data showed. The arrangement allows buyers to access regional supplies without having to independently arrange vessels for the entire journey from within the Gulf. For HPCL, the ability to procure crude and secure transportation for it remain distinct challenges.

items.title: China copper premium hits record as market weighs US stock shift
items.original_title: China copper premium hits record as market weighs US stock shift

The market is facing competing pressures, with expectations that easing US tariff risks could release more metal into the international market and pressure futures prices, while physical tightness in China continues to support spot premiums and demand for imported cathode. China’s copper cathode import premium rose to an all-time high Nov. Platts, part of S&P Global Energy, assessed the Chinese copper import premium at $220/metric ton over the London Metal Exchange cash price, CIF China, on Nov. The record premium comes as market participants reassess international copper flows following the US midterm elections, with China-based market participants increasingly expecting a potential delay or moderation in US tariffs on refined copper imports in 2027. items.title: Stowaway prevention: best practice
items.original_title: Stowaway prevention: best practice
items.summary: Stowaways remain a significant security and operational risk for vessels calling at ports in West Africa. Two recent cases handled by Skuld once again highlight the persistent stowaway risk in the region and the importance of conducting thorough and systematic physical searches. Even where professional third-party security services and trained search dogs are employed, the vessel’s own search remains a critical element of effective stowaway prevention. Best practices For vessels calling at ports with an elevated stowaway risk, Skuld recommends a layered approach centred on access control and systematic physical searches. Importantly, sufficient time must be allocated for each stowaway search. Ultimately, effective stowaway prevention depends not on completing a checklist or obtaining a search certificate, but on ensuring that the vessel has been thoroughly searched. Loss prevention recommendations The company should establish clear stowaway search procedures appropriate to each vessel’s trade, type and operating conditions. Effective implementation of the above best practices and recommendations can significantly reduce the risk of stowaways gaining access to or remaining undetected on board. A well-planned and properly executed stowaway prevention programme not only reduces the likelihood of operational disruption, delay and associated costs, but also contributes to the safety and security of the vessel and her crew throughout the voyage.

items.title: South Korea tests Arctic shipping route amid Russia-West row
items.original_title: South Korea tests Arctic shipping route amid Russia-West row
items.summary: A South Korean container ship completed a voyage to Western Europe through the Arctic Ocean off the northern coast of Russia in October, fueling Seoul’s hopes of exploiting the route as a shortcut for trade. The ship made the round trip from Busan to Rotterdam in just 50 days, saving at least 10 days compared to the fastest travel times along the more commonly used Suez Canal route. The Northern Sea Route (NSR) is not only around 7,000 kilometers (4,350 miles) shorter, it also avoids the geopolitical flashpoint of the Middle East. One of the reasons for South Korea testing the Arctic route is its undoubtedly large economic potential. “In addition to potentially lowering shipping costs and transit times, the route’s development could strengthen Busan’s position as a regional maritime hub and create opportunities for South Korea’s shipbuilding sector.” The Lee government has outlined plans for regular commercial services on the NSR by 2030, with the first Korean ship to complete the voyage merely a test of the logistics. Fears of ‘strategic dependency’ The danger, however, is that by developing the NSR as South Korea’s favored route to Europe, “it could introduce a new form of strategic dependency on Russia as Moscow exercises considerable control over navigation along its Arctic coastline,” said Kristanto.

items.title: Turkey’s coal dependence faces scrutiny as COP31 climate summit begins
items.original_title: Turkey’s coal dependence faces scrutiny as COP31 climate summit begins
items.summary: Turkey’s reliance on coal is facing renewed scrutiny ahead of the COP31 climate summit, as communities affected by mining operations urge world leaders to examine the environmental damage linked to the country’s largest electricity source. The United Nations climate conference begins Monday in Antalya and runs through November 20, with the transition toward cleaner energy among the central issues under discussion. Residents of Ikizkoy, near the Akbelen forest in southwestern Mugla province, want delegates to visit communities affected by decades of lignite mining and the expansion of nearby coal operations. Coal generated 34% of Turkey’s electricity last year, making the country Europe’s largest producer of coal-fired power, according to energy research group Ember. Mining operations around Akbelen supply the Yenikoy and Kemerkoy power plants, which together generate slightly more than 2% of Turkey’s electricity. Turkey is proposing a voluntary global electrification target at COP31, although its climate benefits would depend on whether additional electricity comes from low-carbon sources. Energy Minister Alparslan Bayraktar acknowledged the difficulties of reducing coal dependence, citing thousands of jobs supported by mining operations. Ankara considers nuclear power a major alternative and aims to develop 10 gigawatts of nuclear generation capacity by 2040, roughly equivalent to the country’s current coal-powered output.

By comparison, only 25 ports were actively offering methanol bunkering. Those investing in ammonia- and hydrogen-capable ships face a far less mature infrastructure landscape. Singapore began licensing methanol suppliers from January 2026, while Shanghai recorded a single biomethanol transfer of 8,016 tonnes in August 2026. The scale-up has been dramatic, with single methanol transfers increasing from 475 tonnes at Antwerp-Bruges in 2023 to 8,016 tonnes in Shanghai in 2026. The acquisition is one of Alfa Laval’s most significant transactions to date, establishing Alfa Laval as a leading maritime digital platform. NAVTOR will become part of the Ocean Division, and the NAVTOR platform will be consolidated with the StormGeo and PortChain platforms, that are already part of Alfa Laval’s digital fleet solutions portfolio. NAVTOR’s e-navigation and performance solutions will give Alfa Laval a strong product position across on-vessel software deployment as well as performance and route optimization across the global fleet. “With this acquisition, Alfa Laval will expand its digital offering at a time when real-time decision-making is increasingly complex. NAVTOR’s technology and strong footprint complement our maritime digital platform and will strengthen the customer offering,” says Tom Erixon, President and CEO of Alfa Laval. NAVTOR has broad commercial maritime coverage and provides a ship-to-shore ecosystem for vessel owners and operators, making it mission-critical across the digital maritime workflow. As part of the transaction, cover to protect Alfa Laval for these pre-acquisition liabilities has been deferred.

Spot prices of mainstream products at Qingdao port fell by about 3 yuan/mt on average. Iron ore stocks at 35 major Chinese ports stood at 149.13 million mt as of 6 November, up 1.08 million mt week-on-week, according to SMM. Arrivals are expected to recover next week, and port stocks may build further. On the demand side, average daily port outbound volume at the 35 ports fell 55,000 mt week-on-week to 3.12 million mt. Hot metal output at steel mills declined, and outbound volumes weakened with it. Momentum from the earlier short-covering rebound has faded, and pressure from the port stock build remains, limiting upside for futures. Iron ore prices are likely to turn range-bound at high levels in the short term, a downgrade from yesterday’s slightly firmer view.

items.title: Tanker Fleet Growth Threatens Freight Boom, Bullish Secondhand Markets: Analysts
items.original_title: Tanker Fleet Growth Threatens Freight Boom, Bullish Secondhand Markets: Analysts
items.summary: A wave of tanker deliveries is set to test whether geopolitical disruption and longer trading routes can continue supporting charter rates and ship values, according to S&P Global Energy CERA’s latest fleet outlook, after an extraordinary freight market rally pushed some secondhand ship values above newbuilding order prices. Taking newbuild order books and scrapping into account, CERA analysts forecast global tanker capacity will rise from 703.72 million deadweight tons at the end of 2025 to 743.56 million dwt in 2026, 778.35 million dwt in 2027 and 830.61 million dwt in 2028, before reaching 862.98 million dwt in 2029. That would represent cumulative growth of 22.6% over four years. “The critical issue is not whether supply will grow, it clearly will, but whether ton-mile demand, scrapping, sanctions-related inefficiencies and operational segmentation can absorb that growth without a material decline in utilization and freight rates.” Record rates Tanker rates across segments have risen to record levels following the outbreak of the US-Iran war at the end of February, boosted by increased ship requirements as Asian importers seek barrels from farther afield and Middle Eastern producers rely on ship-to-ship transfers to mitigate transit risks around the Strait of Hormuz. Product tanker deliveries are more front-loaded, with Aframax/Long Range 2 and Medium Range growth expected to moderate after 2026-2027.

items.title: Ethanol-Fuelled Vessels Enter Dry Bulk Orderbook As Owners Seek Fuel Flexibility
items.original_title: Ethanol-Fuelled Vessels Enter Dry Bulk Orderbook As Owners Seek Fuel Flexibility
items.summary: These questions have become more relevant. Although the first methanol/ethanol-capable dry bulk vessels entered the orderbook in 2023, they gained popularity from May 2026, and the number increased to 19 vessels by September. The wider trend is equally interesting. LNG accounted for most of the alternative-fuel vessels in the dry bulk orderbook four years ago. The 19 methanol/ethanol-capable vessels currently in the dry bulk orderbook are linked to Vale’s move towards fuel-flexible ore carriers, with multiple shipowners ordering these vessels against long-term employment with the miner. Major cargo owners could also influence this shift if they increasingly include fuel capability and emissions in chartering decisions as they seek to reduce their Scope 3 emissions. Conclusion Nineteen methanol/ethanol-capable vessels on the orderbook do not signal a rapid shift towards ethanol. Instead, it shows that some owners have started paying for flexibility while the industry still lacks clarity on future fuel economics and regulations. For dry bulk shipping, this could ultimately create greater differentiation within the fleet.

items.summary: From January 1, 2018 to October 9, 2026, Windward MIOC analysis of 52 PRC research vessels shows several distinct changes in where and how the fleet works. The northern South China Sea’s share of fleet working time (slow-speed survey and station work offshore) rose from 22% in 2019–21 to 41% in 2023–25. China Geological Survey and academic vessels account for 78% of the added time, mainly over offshore oil, gas and gas-hydrate areas. In 2026, Effort Moved Toward Taiwan Jan–Sep working time within 300 NM of Taiwan rose from 3,862 to 7,411 hours compared with the same period in 2025, roughly doubling on both the Taiwan, Japan and the Philippines side and the mainland side, while fleet working time overall stayed roughly flat. Near Japan’s southwestern islands, slow-speed working time rose about eightfold, and the vessels involved match Japan Coast Guard reports of unauthorized survey activity. Instead faster seabed mapping around Guam increased in 2024. Field Program or Sustained Reallocation: Too Early to Tell There is a roughly even chance the 2026 increase around Taiwan reflects a recurring spring and summer field program rather than a sustained reallocation of effort. Activity through the winter and in spring 2027 will help distinguish between the two.

items.original_title: North Korean cargo ships crowd Russia’s Nakhodka amid coal, arms suspicions
items.summary: Last month, North Korean cargo ships repeatedly went in and out of the Russian Far East’s Nakhodka port. Because many were spotted around coal terminals and sanctioned vessels were among them, suspicions are being raised that trades are taking place to conceal the origin of North Korean coal. According to U.S.-based North Korea–focused outlet NK News on the 5th (local time), MarineTraffic ship-tracking data showed at least 13 North Korean ships recorded 14 visits to Nakhodka in October. North Korean ship visits to Nakhodka tallied through early November this year totaled 20, 14 of which were concentrated in October. Of the 13 North Korean ships that sent position signals near Nakhodka last month, at least nine were around coal terminals. Experts offered several possibilities for why North Korean ships have been turning up one after another at Russia’s coal terminals. Another notable point is the larger size of North Korean ships calling at Nakhodka this year. Whereas small fishing boats and refrigerated carriers mainly visited last year, large cargo ships have markedly increased this year. This raises the possibility that as North Korea–Russia trade expands, larger ships have been deployed, as well as the possibility of weapons transport.

items.original_title: EU Lawmakers Push Back Against Approval of Indian Ship Recycling Yards
items.summary: A Maersk Line containership seen alongside other ships a Hong Kong Convention-approved ship recycling facility in Alang, India. Photo credit: Maersk A European Parliament committee has voted to oppose the approval of two Indian ship recycling yards, dealing a setback to shipping industry efforts to expand access to South Asia’s shipbreaking facilities. The Parliament’s Environment Committee voted Wednesday to object to the European Commission’s proposal to add Shree Ram Vessel Scrap and YSI Recyclers, both located in Alang-Sosiya, Gujarat, to the European List of approved ship recycling facilities. The two yards had received preliminary backing from the European Commission following inspections intended to determine whether they meet the requirements of the EU Ship Recycling Regulation. The associations argue that the facilities have invested heavily in infrastructure, worker safety and environmental management, and that rejecting yards found compliant through the Commission’s inspection process would undermine the credibility of the EU approval system. “The inclusion of the two Indian yards in the EU list is a long-awaited and very welcome step, which rewards investments made to meet EU standards,” ECSA Secretary General Sotiris Raptis said in an October 28 statement . More than 95% of global ship recycling takes place in Bangladesh, India, Pakistan and Turkey, according to the shipping associations.

items.title: Finland Sees Continued Demand for Icebreakers Despite Warming Winters, Citing Security Concerns
items.original_title: Finland Sees Continued Demand for Icebreakers Despite Warming Winters, Citing Security Concerns
items.summary: The Finnish multipurpose icebreaker Nordica will support the Canadian Coast Guard under a one-year charter, providing icebreaking, search and rescue, ice management, and environmental response services in the Canadian Arctic. (Credit: Arctia) Finland expects to operate at least as many icebreakers in the coming decades as it does today, despite rising temperatures and declining average ice coverage in the Baltic Sea. This is the conclusion of a new government-commissioned report that also highlights growing security requirements and changes in the commercial shipping fleet. The report warns that the gap between a vessel’s theoretical ice classification and its actual operational capability is becoming more pronounced, potentially increasing demand for icebreaker assistance even as average ice conditions become milder. The first priority is the 1970s-built Urho and Sisu , followed by Kontio and Otso in the 2030s and the multipurpose icebreakers Fennica and Nordica in the 2040s. Finland relies heavily on maritime transport, with more than 95% of its foreign trade in goods carried by sea. The report says reliable winter navigation is essential not only for industrial supply chains and security of supply but also for military mobility. The agencies propose further work on the legal and procurement arrangements by the end of 2026.

items.title: Calmer waters for container spot rates, but ‘fragile’ Middle East a threat
items.original_title: Calmer waters for container spot rates, but ‘fragile’ Middle East a threat
items.summary: There was a certain sense of calm about the container spot freight rate market this week, with slight declines on both the transpacific and Asia-Europe trades as capacity constraints eased and demand remained seasonally subdued. Drewry’s World Container Index (WCI) recorded a 2% week-on-week drop on its Shanghai-Rotterdam leg, to end at $3,615 per 40ft, while the Shanghai-Genoa was flat at $4,166 per 40ft, which indicated that new FAK (freight all kinds) levels, introduced by carriers on 1 November, were unable to stick. The carriers had aimed to push the Asia-North Europe spot rate up to around $4,500 per 40ft and to around $5,000 on Mediterranean shipments. A further attempt at higher FAK levels, around the same as before, is scheduled for 15 November, but modest demand and ample capacity is likely to weigh against them, European forwarders told The Loadstar . “On Asia-Europe rates, we did have initial rates for the fist half of November extended from mid-October, but these are starting to drop a little – I suppose, with the early Chinese New Year, carriers are expecting a small peak, but bookings at this stage would suggest it will not be like previous years,” one said.

items.title: ‘Carrier selection matters’ when it comes to getting your goods on time
items.original_title: ‘Carrier selection matters’ when it comes to getting your goods on time
items.summary: The Asia-North America tradelane is facing the highest ocean freight disruption risk over the coming weeks. Reduced carrier capacity and growing difficulty securing bookings threaten shipment reliability, according to WiseTech Global. The company’s November Ocean Freight Risk Outlook, released today covering weeks 45-48, rates the Asia-North America and Asia-Europe trades as high-risk overall, with Europe-North America assessed as medium risk. It explains that on the transpacific, planned carrier capacity is expected to tighten in the second half of November, driven by reduced supply rather than stronger demand. Booking security risk is also expected to climb to 71% by week 48, well above its historical average of 41%, suggesting growing difficulty securing space on preferred sailings. The latest weekly performance was just 6.5% on time, while 39.1% of arrivals saw delays of eight days or more. Shipment transit time reliability also fell across both Asian tradelanes in October, reaching 21% on Asia-North America, down six percentage points month on month, and 35% on Asia-Europe, a five-point decline. However, on-time performance fell from 39.2% in September to 34.8% in October, while the latest weekly result dropped to 24.6%. Transit-time reliability also weakened, falling three percentage points to 46%.

items.title: Cargo crime in North America down in Q3, but losses are mounting
items.original_title: Cargo crime in North America down in Q3, but losses are mounting
items.summary: Organised criminal networks are increasingly exploiting identity fraud, carrier impersonation and weaknesses in freight verification, driving cargo theft losses across Canada and the US up 39% year on year, despite a sharp decline in reported incidents Verisk CargoNet recorded 2,072 of reported supply chain crime incidents across the countries through to 23 October, marking a 25% decrease in total numbers from the 2,755 recorded during the comparable period in 2025. VP operations at Verisk CargoNet Keith Lewis told The Loadstar : “But while the number of incidents declined, the financial impact moved in the opposite direction, losses increasing 39% to $718.9m.” Furthermore, he noted that the average documented value of stolen goods had also registered a massive surge, 72% year on year, from approximately $261,000 to more than $448,000. Over the third quarter, CargoNet recorded 547 incidents, approximately 33% fewer than a year earlier, but estimated losses still reached $230.1m, with California accounting for the largest share, with 182 incidents, followed by New Jersey, Texas, and Illinois. Among the biggest concerns are fictitious pickups, where criminals impersonate legitimate carriers to collect and divert shipments, with CargoNet recording 138 such incidents in Q3, compared with 147 over the same period of 2025.

items.title: Hong Kong reviews river fees as mainland ports lure cargo away
items.original_title: Hong Kong reviews river fees as mainland ports lure cargo away
items.summary: Hong Kong is reviewing permit fees charged to river trade vessels as it seeks to maintain its port’s competitiveness amid growing competition from mainland Chinese terminals in Guangzhou and Shenzhen. The secretary for transport and logistics, Chan Mei-po, announced the review in a written reply to the Legislative Council on Wednesday. China-flagged vessels carry containers between ports in the Pearl River Delta and Hong Kong, where cargo may be transferred to ocean-going vessels for onward shipment. Hong Kong operates a multiple-entry permit scheme, allowing operators to make up to 10 port entries within a month for a fee equivalent to five single-entries – the “buy five, get five free” system. Ms Chan said: “The Action Plan on Maritime and Port Development Strategy proposes various measures to strengthen Hong Kong’s position as a regional transhipment hub, including reviewing the permit fees charged to river trade vessels in order to maintain the competitiveness and attractiveness of the port to the industry. We have completed a preliminary review and are now discussing the matter with relevant departments, with the details to be released in due course.” Laden container movements between Hong Kong and mainland China account for more than 40% of the territory’s annual laden container throughput.

items.title: Khalid Hashim set to pass the baton at Precious Shipping
items.original_title: Khalid Hashim set to pass the baton at Precious Shipping
items.summary: Thailand’s Precious Shipping is preparing a change at the top, with longtime managing director Khalid Moinuddin Hashim moving to executive vice chairman and finance chief Gautam Khurana taking over the running of the Bangkok-listed dry bulk owner. The company’s board approved the leadership reshuffle, with both appointments taking effect on January 1, 2027, according to a filing with the Stock Exchange of Thailand. Khurana will continue to serve as director of finance until a successor is appointed. The transition marks a significant shift for Precious Shipping, which has been led by Hashim for more than three decades. The management shake-up comes amid a major fleet renewal programme that has seen Precious sell ageing handysize and supramax vessels while expanding its ultramax fleet. In September, the company returned to China’s Taizhou Sanfu Ship Engineering for four 64,500 dwt ultramax newbuildings worth a combined $141.8m, with deliveries scheduled between April 2030 and January 2031. The order followed an earlier $133.46m contract for four 63,500 dwt ultramaxes at the same yard, with two vessels already in service and the remaining pair due through the first quarter of 2027. Once the outstanding newbuildings arrive, Precious expects its fleet to reach 47 vessels totalling about 2.34m dwt.

items.summary: Appalling conditions, unpaid wages and the constant threat of attack: Thousands of sailors are stranded in the Strait of Hormuz as the US-Iran conflict disrupts shipping routes and experts warn of risks to global trade. The Strait of Hormuz, one of the world’s most important shipping routes, has become a dangerous war zone due to the conflict between Iran and the United States, leaving thousands of seafarers stranded and exposing them to missile and mine attacks. According to the International Transport Workers’ Federation, many crews face severe shortages of food, drinking water, fuel, medical assistance, and unpaid wages, while more than 40 sailors have reportedly been killed. The organization criticizes some shipowners for continuing to send vessels into the high-risk area despite the obvious dangers to crews. Shipping companies such as Hapag-Lloyd say they have prioritized crew safety over profits, rerouting ships and accepting significant financial losses to avoid conflict zones. items.title: Singapore and Norway Launch Joint Research Grant Call to Advance Greener Shipping
items.original_title: Singapore and Norway Launch Joint Research Grant Call to Advance Greener Shipping
items.summary: The Maritime and Port Authority of Singapore (MPA), the Research Council of Norway (RCN) and the Singapore Maritime Institute (SMI) have launched a joint research grant call to develop solutions to support the decarbonisation of international shipping. The joint grant call brings together the research, technology and industry capabilities of Singapore’s and Norway’s maritime innovation ecosystems to address shared technological and operational challenges and develop solutions applicable across international shipping. The grant call builds on the MPA-RCN Memorandum of Understanding signed in April 2024 on maritime research, development, education and training. The grant call will focus on three areas: · Alternative fuels and energy infrastructure: Improving the safety and handling of alternative marine fuels, developing bunkering and fuel storage technologies, and advancing charging infrastructure for electric vessels. · Digitalisation and greener shipping operations: Advancing voyage optimisation, just-in-time arrivals, autonomous operations and ship-port data exchange to improve operational efficiency and reduce emissions. SMI will provide up to S$2.7 million for Singapore research partners, while RCN will make available up to NOK 20 million for Norwegian research partners. Launched at the International Association of Ports and Harbors World Ports Conference, the State of Port Digital Readiness & Stakeholder Adoption of Port Community Systems report found half of respondents identified customs as the primary barrier to adoption, while 35 per cent cited other government agencies. “Ports are facing greater supply chain disruption, congestion, labour volatility, and compliance demands, but technology alone cannot solve these pressures while information remains fragmented between organisations and regulatory systems,” said Vineet Malhotra, Co-Founder and Director, Kalé. “The next phase of port digitalisation requires policy, people, and technology to move together, with authorities enabling trusted data exchange and ensuring developing markets are not left behind.” PCS connect public and private organisations across a port through a shared digital environment, allowing data to be securely exchanged and reused to reduce paperwork, congestion, delays, and duplicated processes, while improving cargo visibility and coordination. It finds 79 per cent of respondents report that their port does not have a fully operational PCS, while 22 per cent highlighted digital skills gaps as a barrier to adoption, and uptake remains particularly weak in low-income countries.

items.title: Advancing maritime digitalization in West and Central Africa
items.original_title: Advancing maritime digitalization in West and Central Africa
items.summary: The digitalization of ports across nine West and Central African countries has been boosted through a regional workshop in Accra, Ghana. The event was organized by IMO, the Africa Transport Policy Program (SSATP), and the World Bank, in partnership with the Ghana Maritime Authority. The key aims of the event included: • Promoting the adoption of the IMO Compendium on Facilitation and Electronic Business, which sets out how shipping and port data are structured and shared electronically to streamline communication; and • Scaling up the implementation of Maritime Single Windows (MSWs) and Port Community Systems (PCSs), which are integrated digital platforms that streamline vessel and cargo clearance, reduce bureaucratic delays, and will help to strengthen Africa’s competitiveness in global maritime trade. Promoting regional collaboration The workshop convened regional and international institutions committed to translating policy into action, including the Port Management Association of West and Central Africa (PMAWCA), the African Development Bank (AfDB), the African Harbour Masters’ Committee (AHMC), and the African Alliance for Electronic Commerce (AAEC). The workshop was structured around both knowledge sharing and practical capacity building, with 55 participants, including 15 women, from maritime administrations, port authorities, and customs authorities in Cabo Verde, Equatorial Guinea, The Gambia, Ghana, Guinea-Bissau, Liberia, Nigeria, São Tomé and Príncipe, and Sierra Leone.

Alfa Laval described the purchase as one of the most significant transactions in its history. Alfa Laval said it expects the business to generate about $194m in revenue this year. “With this acquisition, Alfa Laval will expand its digital offering at a time when real-time decision-making is increasingly complex,” said chief executive Tom Erixon. US technology investor Accel-KKR took a majority stake in NAVTOR in 2020, followed by purchases of performance analytics specialist Tres Solutions in 2021 and digital logbook developer Ingenium Marine in 2022. NAVTOR then combined with Voyager Worldwide in 2023, creating a business whose technology at the time served about 18,000 vessels. Alfa Laval has been assembling its own maritime software stack since buying weather routing and voyage optimisation company StormGeo for NOK3.63bn in 2021. items.title: Indian ship recycling breakthrough hits Brussels roadblock
items.original_title: Indian ship recycling breakthrough hits Brussels roadblock
items.summary: A European Parliament committee has voted against allowing two Indian shipbreaking yards onto the EU’s approved recycling list, dealing a setback to shipowners pushing for greater access to South Asian dismantling capacity. The Parliament’s environment committee backed an objection this week to the European Commission’s proposal to approve Shree Ram Vessel Scrap and YSI Recyclers, both located in the Alang-Sosiya shipbreaking hub in Gujarat. The two facilities had received preliminary backing from the Commission following inspections intended to establish whether they met the requirements of the EU Ship Recycling Regulation. Their inclusion would make them the first facilities on the Indian subcontinent to join the European list. Environmental organisations and recycling industry representatives have taken the opposite position, arguing that beaching operations cannot provide sufficient containment of hazardous materials and should not qualify for EU recognition. Campaigners have also challenged the industry’s argument that additional capacity is needed, pointing to more than 2m light displacement tonnes of combined annual capacity at facilities already on the EU list, which they claim is sufficient to handle recent recycling volumes involving EU-flagged and EU-owned ships. Under EU rules, EU-flagged commercial ships subject to the Ship Recycling Regulation must be dismantled at facilities on the approved European list.

items.title: Shipping has a coffee problem
items.original_title: Shipping has a coffee problem
items.summary: From Posidonia to Geneva Dry, the shipping industry’s favourite pastime appears to be arranging coffee meetings that may or may not actually happen. Mike Darby from Merchant Recruitment makes the case for the Baltic Flat White Index. In bunkering, the cappuccino effect means paying for froth instead of fuel. I’m increasingly convinced that approximately 70% of the shipping industry is trying to arrange a coffee with the other 30%. Then there’s the person who manages to arrange eight coffee meetings between 9am and midday. An impressive achievement considering each meeting is apparently going to last 30 minutes, nobody knows where they’re meeting and the exhibition centre is roughly the size of a small European country. By 4pm, the original coffee meeting has somehow turned into drinks, dinner and a discussion about whether anyone actually knows who’s paying. Then there’s the classic closing line: ”We must do this more often.” Which, translated into shipping language, means we’ll probably bump into each other in Athens next June, promise to arrange another coffee and repeat the entire process. Shipping remains a relationship-driven industry, and despite all the technology, digitalisation and virtual meetings, there’s still something valuable about sitting down with someone face-to-face.

items.title: Seven Shadow Fleet Tankers Spoof AIS to Hide Novorossiysk Voyages
items.original_title: Seven Shadow Fleet Tankers Spoof AIS to Hide Novorossiysk Voyages
items.summary: Sanctioned Tankers Fake Their Positions Near the Bosphorus A cluster of seven sanctioned Russian tankers were found to have routinely and deliberately manipulated AIS over the past 90 days to falsely claim they were drifting off the Black Sea close to the Bosphorus entrance. The tankers were instead identified by Windward clandestinely sailing for the Russian oil terminal of Novorossiysk to load oil, hugging the Black Sea coastline to try and avoid Ukrainian drone attacks. At the same time, the tankers manipulated their AIS, a process known as spoofing. Windward Identifies Seven Sanctioned Shadow Fleet Tankers The vessels identified were a Sierra Leone-flagged Suezmax tanker, a Russia-flagged Aframax, a Russia-flagged Aframax tanker, an Equatorial Guinea-flagged Suezmax, an Equatorial Guinea-flagged Aframax, a Comoros-flagged Suezmax, and a Russia-flagged Aframax tanker. All are sanctioned, shadow fleet vessels. Periods of GNSS manipulation lasted around 2-3 weeks, the duration for tankers to sail to Novorossiysk, load, and return. While many vessels are switching off their AIS for legitimate safety and security reasons in the Black Sea, Russian shadow fleet tankers are using deceptive shipping practices, including GNSS manipulation, to avoid targeting by Ukrainian drones. A further seven cargo ships were damaged in attacks attributed to Russia off Bulgaria and Romania just outside their territorial waters over October.

items.title: Inmarsat Maritime Safety Data Hub to help shipping weather the storm
items.original_title: Inmarsat Maritime Safety Data Hub to help shipping weather the storm
items.summary: As the maritime threat landscape continues to evolve, so too must the quality of information available to the industry. Inmarsat Maritime recently launched the Maritime Safety Data Hub, which combines Global Maritime Distress and Safety System (GMDSS) call data with an industry-first analysis of maritime safety broadcasts. Complementing this unique dataset is a series of interviews with maritime safety experts conducted by Inmarsat’s research partner, SeaFocus International, as part of the Safety Hub’s development. Managing weather hazards Among the 106,975 maritime safety broadcasts made in 2025, 2.6% were marked ‘urgent’. Having access to more granular data on a vessel’s vulnerability to extreme weather can therefore help crew avoid distress situations. Persistent challenges, evolving risks While Inmarsat received fewer GMDSS calls in 2025 (741) than in 2023 (788) and 2024 (801), the three-year trend remains broadly consistent with historical averages, reflecting how established safety challenges persist even as new risks emerge. A powerful new layer of maritime intelligence The Inmarsat Maritime Safety Data Hub will enable the industry to better understand the factors affecting maritime safety and adopt a more proactive approach to risk management, commented John Dodd, Head of Maritime Safety at Inmarsat Maritime. “The value of maritime safety information lies in giving ships and shipping operators the time to make informed decisions,” he said.

items.title: US copper cathode imports to slow in November as October beats breakbulk record
items.original_title: US copper cathode imports to slow in November as October beats breakbulk record
items.summary: US breakbulk imports of copper cathode are on track to exceed 230kt in October, a monthly record, but Kpler expects deliveries to fall to 100kt in November now that the LME–COMEX arbitrage has closed. The pending Section 232 tariff verdict will decide whether the US draws in more copper, and what happens to the estimated 2 million tons of cathode already on US shores. Record-breaking imports October deliveries of copper cathode in breakbulk are on track to exceed 230kt as the month draws to a close. Once containerised and overland trade is fully accounted for, Kpler estimates that the US will have imported over 800kt in the last 4 months, a figure on par with average annual imports prior to 2025. Chile has remained the primary source of breakbulk cathode deliveries in recent months, but the swing tons have come from the DRC and, to a lesser extent, Zambia, with African ports supplying 243kt since the start of July, compared to just 97kt in the first half of the year. Chinese imports of Chilean cathode have fallen from 48kt per month in 2024 to around 15kt since the arbitrage first opened in 2025. With seaborne imports of copper concentrate down 11% year-to-date and restrictions impacting the availability of scrap, the Chinese market is in short supply.

items.title: MARAD Approves $1 Billion Offshore Crude Oil Export Port Off Louisiana
items.original_title: MARAD Approves $1 Billion Offshore Crude Oil Export Port Off Louisiana
items.summary: The Trump administration has approved a $1 billion offshore crude oil export project off the coast of Louisiana, clearing a major regulatory hurdle for a facility designed to load some of the world’s largest oil tankers directly in the Gulf of Mexico. U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy announced Thursday that the Maritime Administration (MARAD) has approved the deepwater port license application for Blue Marlin Offshore Port, a project capable of exporting up to 2 million barrels of crude oil per day. The project, developed by an affiliate of Energy Transfer, will use existing and converted offshore platform infrastructure connected to crude oil supply hubs in Texas and southwest Louisiana. The approval is the fourth deepwater port project cleared under the Trump administration, following the Texas GulfLink crude oil export project, Delfin LNG off Louisiana, and the $8.2 billion ST LNG project approved off Texas last week. Blue Marlin is also the second crude oil export project approved since President Trump issued his Unleashing American Energy executive order in January 2025. Just last week, MARAD announced approval of an $8.2 billion deepwater LNG export project off the Texas coast, saying changes to its licensing process had shortened the review timeline.

items.title: IMO Backs Dominguez for Second Term Amid Shipping Attacks and Climate Deadlock
items.original_title: IMO Backs Dominguez for Second Term Amid Shipping Attacks and Climate Deadlock
items.summary: IMO Secretary-General Arsenio Dominguez at the opening of the IMO Marine Environment Protection Committee (MEPC) 2nd extraordinary session, 14-17 October, 2025. Photo courtesy IMO The International Maritime Organization (IMO) Council has backed Secretary-General Arsenio Dominguez for a second four-year term, extending its support for his leadership despite the organization’s failure to adopt its landmark Net-Zero Framework and an escalating security crisis threatening commercial shipping. The decision, announced Wednesday during the Council’s 138th session in London, would extend Dominguez’s mandate from January 1, 2028, through December 31, 2031, subject to formal approval by the IMO Assembly in late 2027. “I am deeply grateful to the Members of the Council and all Members of the Organization for their continued trust and support,” Dominguez said in an IMO statement . The endorsement comes at a particularly challenging time for the UN maritime agency, which has struggled to build consensus on climate regulations while confronting mounting threats to freedom of navigation and the safety of seafarers. Dominguez presided over a major setback in October 2025, when IMO member states failed to formally adopt the organization’s proposed Net-Zero Framework, a landmark package of global fuel standards and greenhouse gas emissions pricing measures for international shipping, amid pressure from the United States and other oil-producing countries.

items.title: Maersk’s 26-Ship LNG Order Adds Nearly Half a Million TEU to Newbuilding Pipeline
items.original_title: Maersk’s 26-Ship LNG Order Adds Nearly Half a Million TEU to Newbuilding Pipeline
items.summary: FILE PHOTO: Containers are seen on the Maersk's Triple-E giant container ship Majestic Maersk as it sails in the Strait of Gibraltar towards the port of Algeciras, Spain January 19, 2023. Moller-Maersk is pressing ahead with one of its largest containership ordering programs in years, confirming in its third-quarter earnings report that it has ordered 26 LNG dual-fuel vessels with a combined capacity of nearly 484,000 TEU. The order, first confirmed by Maersk in September, represents 483,600 TEU of newbuilding capacity, equivalent to roughly 10% of the carrier’s existing operating fleet. As gCaptain reported this week , a new Lloyd’s Register study found that LNG bunkering was available at 222 ports worldwide, compared with just 25 ports offering methanol. The disparity helps explain why LNG continues to dominate alternative-fuel newbuilding orders despite questions about its long-term climate benefits. While Maersk describes the latest contracts as part of its ongoing renewal program, the 26 ships represent a substantial addition to its construction pipeline at a time when major rivals including MSC, CMA CGM and COSCO are also investing heavily in new tonnage. The company’s third-quarter operating profit rose sharply to $2.6 billion, up from $567 million a year earlier, with fleet utilization reaching 96%.

items.title: Port of Long Beach set to handle record 10m teu this year
items.original_title: Port of Long Beach set to handle record 10m teu this year
items.summary: The Californian port of Long Beach is predicted to handle more than 10m teu this year, for the first time. “It’s been a peak year,” Port of Long Beach CEO Noel Hacegaba told The Loadstar on the sidelines of the World Ports Conference in London this week. His comments followed a record-breaking September, when throughput hit 997,177 teu, its busiest month ever, surpassing the previous record set in October 2024. Dr Hacegaba said the very strong growth in transpacific volumes had been due to a combination of shippers front-loading imports to avoid the threatened USTR 301 port fees on Chinese-owned and -operated vessels, concerns about the viability of the Panama Canal as El Nino emerged, and fuel costs. The cargo surge had led to MSC deploying some of its largest ships, of 24,000 teu capacity, on its standalone transpacific Sentosa service, which calls at Long Beach’s Total Terminal International (TTI) facility “Normally the ships on this service are smaller, but we have handled some of their largest ships, with 100% discharging and 100% loading – this is a glimpse of our future,” Dr Hacegaba said.

items.title: US importers should reconsider farming out customs paperwork, warns CargoTrans
items.original_title: US importers should reconsider farming out customs paperwork, warns CargoTrans
items.summary: US importers using ‘delivered duty-paid’ (DDP) shipping arrangements face increasing compliance and financial risks, as Customs and Border Protection (CBP) intensifies its scrutiny of foreign importers of record, according to CargoTrans. Nunzio De Filippis, co-CEO, and Rennie Alston, director of trade compliance, warned that US buyers could face penalties, shipment seizures, and refused entries, even when the firm is not named as the importer of record. During CargoTrans’s latest monthly Tariff Tea webinar, the executives said the post-Liberation Day rush towards DDP arrangements was beginning to reverse, as importers reconsidered the risks of handing control of customs formalities to overseas suppliers. However, Mr Alston warned: “If you are the US consignee, if you are the US order party, if you are the instigator to the transaction, then you have culpability.” CargoTrans said CBP was increasingly investigating whether DDP arrangements were being used to avoid tariffs, particularly where foreign sellers or intermediary platforms acted as non-resident importers of record. He also raised concerns about the growing volume of CBP requests for information, known as CF28s, and urged importers to investigate their records thoroughly before responding. Mr Alston said companies should avoid rushing to meet the standard 20-day response deadline, without first checking the information internally across their procurement, finance, legal, compliance, and logistics teams.

While the Danish shipping and logistics group said revenue growth had been driven by all its divisions, Ocean Services accounted for the largest contribution, some $12.6bn, an increase of 37% on the same period last year. Group CEO Vincent Clerc said: “We delivered a strong quarter across our businesses. Despite continued geopolitical uncertainty and disruptions, global trade has remained remarkably resilient.” Average loaded freight rates increased 46% year on year, to $3,287 per 40ft, with Mr Clerc singling out investment in electrification, energy, and AI infrastructure as one of the core drivers of growth. The rate increase offset moderate volume declines, added the company, down 0.8% over the three-month period to 3.37m feu, which Maersk attributed to the severe weather in Asia and the Strait of Hormuz, although volumes were, nevertheless, 0.3% up on the second quarter. Double-digit revenue growth was also forthcoming for Logistics & Services, which recorded a 13% upturn in turnover, to $4.5bn, from $4bn a year earlier, while Forwarding saw solid growth in airfreight and project logistics.

items.title: HEA Energy snaps up Subsea7’s six-ship heavy transport business
items.original_title: HEA Energy snaps up Subsea7’s six-ship heavy transport business
items.summary: Abu Dhabi-based HEA Energy has struck a deal to acquire Subsea7’s heavy transportation business, adding a six-vessel operation to its growing offshore fleet. The transaction will see Subsea7’s offshore renewables arm Seaway7 divest a business comprising five owned and one chartered open-deck semi-submersible heavy transport vessels. The fleet includes Seaway Eagle, Seaway Falcon, Seaway Hawk, Seaway Osprey, Seaway Albatross and the chartered Seaway Swan . The vessels are used to transport offshore wind foundations, substations, jackup rigs, offshore modules and other oversized cargo, with lifting and transportation capabilities covering loads of up to 55,000 tonnes. The sale forms part of the permitted divestments under Subsea7’s merger agreement with Italian offshore contractor Saipem and will trigger a €105m special dividend to Subsea7 shareholders. HEA has been building up its offshore support and wind maintenance fleet through newbuildings and acquisitions. The divestment comes as Subsea7 and Saipem work towards their proposed merger to create Saipem7. Brazil’s competition watchdog gave conditional clearance to the combination on November 4, requiring the separate sale of the Seven Borealis pipelay and heavylift vessel to address competition concerns. The proposed merger, which would create an offshore engineering group with combined revenues of about €21bn ($23.6bn), still faces regulatory scrutiny in Europe and Australia.

Its overall fleet stands at 182 vessels, including newbuildings, split between 65 bulkers, 54 containerships and 63 tankers. items.title: Evergreen’s Suez return leaves Zim increasingly isolated
items.original_title: Evergreen’s Suez return leaves Zim increasingly isolated
items.summary: The container shipping industry’s long detour around southern Africa is rapidly coming to an end, with Taiwan’s Evergreen preparing to send its first ships through the Suez Canal after almost three years of avoiding the Red Sea. According to liner consultancy Linerlytica, Evergreen will deploy the 16,556 teu Ever Eon and Ever Edit through Suez on November 7 and 11 respectively, operating on the Ocean Alliance’s NEU7/CES service. The 20,124 teu Ever Gifted will follow on November 16 on the alliance’s MD2 Mediterranean service. Evergreen had been the last Ocean Alliance member holding out against a return to the canal, with partners CMA CGM, Cosco and OOCL already restoring services through the waterway. Meanwhile, Maersk and Hapag-Lloyd have announced that their Gemini Cooperation’s ME1 service linking India and Europe will switch from the Cape of Good Hope, with the first westbound sailing departing Salalah yesterday. items.original_title: Coast Guard Looks to Commercial Icebreakers to Keep Northeast Ports Open This Winter
items.summary: Coast Guard Cutter Penobscot Bay, a 140-foot bay-class icebreaking tug, breaks ice on the Hudson River in support of Operation Reliable Energy for Northeast Winters (OPRENEW), February 11, 2021. OPRENEW is the Coast Guard's effort to keep waterways clear of ice during the winter months. Coast Guard is exploring the use of commercial icebreaking vessels to help keep Northeast ports and waterways open this winter, as the service prepares for another season of potentially disruptive ice conditions. The Coast Guard is looking for vessels capable of operating in ice ranging from 4 to 18 inches thick, with the ability to mobilize to the Northeast by January 2, 2027. The request follows a difficult 2025–2026 winter that saw severe ice conditions across the Northeast and Great Lakes, forcing the Coast Guard to deploy icebreaking assets to maintain commercial navigation. The new commercial vessel initiative also comes as the Coast Guard moves forward with plans to modernize its aging domestic icebreaking fleet. The service is pursuing the acquisition of up to seven Homeland Security Cutter–Light Icebreakers to replace its aging 65-foot icebreaking tugs, which perform critical winter missions throughout the Northeast. The Coast Guard issued a formal solicitation for the new vessels earlier this year, with final proposals due in October.

items.summary: The International Association of Ports and Harbors (IAPH) and the International Port Community Systems Association (IPCSA) signed an MoU today at the 2026 IAPH World Ports Conference held at the ICC Olympia. The agreement aims to build on both organisation’s efforts to promote the digitalisation of ports and maritime supply chains and follows years of collaboration on the topic – most recently at the IMO Facilitation Committee (FAL 50) in April when IPCSA co-sponsored IAPH’s successful proposal to adopt amendments to the FAL Convention to include a mandatory cyber security standard to safeguard Maritime Single Windows (MSW). The MoU was signed at the conclusion of a high-level conference roundtable focused on data harmonisation for Port Call Optimisation (PCO) and supply chain resilience, at which IPCSA Secretary-General Nico De Cauwer was an expert panellist. The panel session included the presentation of A Common Digital Infrastructure Standard for Supply Chain Resilience in Container Ports: Creating Cargo Traceability for Multi-modal Supply Chain Operations, an output of the IAPH Data Collaboration Committee developed with the support of the Supply Chain Resilience Taskforce, of which IPCSA is a key member.

The vessel, formerly known as Phonix, has been linked to Iran’s shadow oil trade. Photo: Department of War The United States on Wednesday sanctioned a network of individuals and companies accused of operating fraudulent ship registries that helped Iran’s shadow fleet evade sanctions, while issuing a new warning to maritime companies about the risks of dealing with falsely flagged vessels. Treasury cited the case of the MAJESTIC X , formerly PHONIX (IMO 9198317), which was seized by U.S. The warning reflects a growing problem in the shadow fleet trade, where vessels increasingly rely on questionable or outright fraudulent registrations after being removed from legitimate flag registries. OFAC said that while shadow fleet operators have long used frequent flag changes to obscure their activities, fraudulent registries have become an increasingly common way to keep sanctioned vessels operating. OFAC also encouraged governments to investigate fraudulent registries operating in their names and report suspected cases to the International Maritime Organization so that maritime databases accurately reflect vessels with invalid registrations. The maritime designations and new OFAC advisory highlight Washington’s growing focus on the service providers and intermediaries that keep Iran’s shadow fleet operating, rather than the tankers themselves.

items.original_title: $100 Million Tanker Dispute Raises Stakes in Mercuria’s Baltic Exchange Lawsuit
items.summary: A wooden plaque is seen on a wall at The Baltic Exchange in the City of London, Britain March 2, 2016. REUTERS/Toby Melville/File Photo, Reuters (Bloomberg) — As lawyers for Mercuria Energy Group presented the commodity giant’s case against the Baltic Exchange this week, a group of smartly dressed Norwegian businessmen listened intently to the arguments from the back of a packed London courtroom. The executives, representing Oslo-listed Hunter Group ASA, have around $100 million riding on the outcome. The company is in a dispute with Mercuria over a charter deal linked to the TD3C index — the global benchmark oil tanker rate that the trading house claims the Baltic Exchange should have suspended because of disruptions caused by the Iran war. “As of now, it’s more than $100 million total accrued charter income, losses and interest,” Hunter Chairman Morten Astrup told Bloomberg News in a London interview. Mercuria says the Baltic Exchange should have suspended the benchmark rate from early March to July 3, when oil flows through the Strait of Hormuz came to a near standstill as Tehran targeted shipping in the waterway linking the Persian Gulf to the rest of the world.

items.title: Wave of feeder newbuilds could bring a chill to charter rates in 2027
items.original_title: Wave of feeder newbuilds could bring a chill to charter rates in 2027
items.summary: Feeder containership charter rates could face downward pressure in 2027 as a wave of newbuild deliveries adds capacity to a market that has enjoyed strong earnings in 2026. Ship brokerage Intermodal research analyst Vasilis Fousekis noted that the time-charter rate for a 1,700 teu geared feeder had climbed to about $33,750 a day for six to 12 months, up 19% year on year and more than double its 2023 level. A 1,000 teu vessel now earns approximately $18,750 a day, up 10% annually. Gemini Cooperation partners Maersk and Hapag-Lloyd, in need of tonnage to support their hub-and-spoke model, were also busy. Maersk fixed the 2000-built 2,442 teu Meratus Jayagiri from Indonesian feeder operator Meratus Line for $26,500 a day for two years, while Hapag-Lloyd chartered Germany’s Hanse Bereederung’s 2023-built 1,930 teu Cape Bruno for $21,250 a day for three years. The feeder orderbook stands at around 1.05m teu, across 635 vessels, equivalent to almost 20% of the existing fleet. Around 42% of the orderbook capacity is scheduled for delivery in 2027, with another 34% set for 2028, mainly in the 1,000–1,999 teu segment. With demolition remaining negligible, despite 30% of feeder capacity being at least 20 years old, fleet growth could reach around 6% next year.
