items.title: Torm strikes eight-tanker newbuild deal in joint venture push
items.original_title: Torm strikes eight-tanker newbuild deal in joint venture push
items.summary: Danish product tanker giant Torm has stepped up its fleet expansion with agreements for eight LR2 newbuildings through a 50:50 joint venture. The Copenhagen- and New York-listed owner disclosed the latest contracts in its third-quarter results, confirming that the agreements were signed after the end of September. Torm has not identified its joint venture partner or the shipyard involved, while pricing and delivery dates for the eight vessels have also been left undisclosed. The original six 50,000 dwt ships are scheduled for delivery in 2029, with the additional pair following in 2030. Shipbroking sources previously placed the scrubber-fitted vessels at around $46m apiece, valuing the full eight-ship programme at approximately $368m. Torm has since secured options for another two MR newbuildings, potentially extending that programme further. The latest investments build on a fleet renewal drive that has also seen the company acquire six MR resale newbuildings scheduled to join its fleet between 2027 and 2028. The owner has meanwhile continued to dispose of older tonnage, selling the 2007-built LR1 Torm Venture and the 2008-built MR Torm Laura during the third quarter. Those disposals left Torm with an operating fleet of 95 product tankers at the end of September, excluding vessels on order.

items.summary: Greek gas shipowner Benelux Overseas has been linked to another pair of midsize gas carriers at China’s Huangpu Wenchong Shipbuilding, adding to its growing orderbook at the CSSC-affiliated yard. Shipbuilding sources have identified the Athens-based company, controlled by Kostas Angelou, as the buyer behind the latest 48,000 cu m two-ship deal, extending a relationship dating back to late 2023. Huangpu Wenchong has confirmed the contract through China Shipbuilding Trading, identifying the customer only as a European shipowner. The ships will feature three independent fully refrigerated Type A cargo tanks, allowing them to carry LPG and ammonia, among other cargoes. Benelux first turned to Huangpu Wenchong in December 2023, ordering two vessels of the same size with an option for a third, which was exercised in March 2024. The initial pair was reported to cost around $64m apiece. The latest deal adds to the Greek owner’s wider gas carrier expansion, which has also included a move into larger ammonia-capable tonnage. Last December, shipbuilding sources linked Benelux to a $240m order for two 93,000 cu m very large ammonia carriers at HD Hyundai Heavy Industries in South Korea, with deliveries scheduled for 2028. Benelux has also sourced gas carrier tonnage from South Korea, including a pair of 40,000 cu m ships contracted at HD Hyundai Mipo in 2021.

items.original_title: Cameroon’s Gulfcam taps new chief to drive Camship expansion
items.summary: Cameroon’s Gulfcam is pursuing plans to acquire six vessels to expand its coastal container shipping operations between Kribi and Douala, with a former Camship executive taking charge of the business. Bernard André Ndengue took over as chief executive on November 1, replacing Albert Roger Boum, who stepped down last month to head Puma Energy’s operations in the Republic of Congo. Ndengue, a veteran of the country’s maritime sector who previously held senior positions at Cameroon Shipping Lines (Camship), has been tasked with developing Gulfcam’s container shipping arm and pushing ahead with its coastal shipping ambitions. The Douala-based group outlined plans in March to acquire six vessels to increase capacity between Cameroon’s two main ports, with the aim of capturing around half of the container freight currently transported by road along the corridor. The planned expansion would cover both domestic coastal trade and transshipment cargo, allowing containers discharged from larger vessels at the deepwater port of Kribi to reach Douala by sea rather than by truck.No investment figure, vessel specifications or acquisition timetable has been disclosed. Gulfcam announced the relaunch of its Camship service earlier this year, bringing in the chartered containership Atlantic Runner II to support operations between the two ports. Gulfcam itself was established in 2021 through the merger of Camship-CLGG and petroleum transport and distribution business Gulfin.

items.title: Greenland’s scrubber ban sparks calls for wider Arctic crackdown
items.original_title: Greenland’s scrubber ban sparks calls for wider Arctic crackdown
items.summary: Greenland is moving to ban scrubber wastewater discharges throughout its territorial waters, prompting environmental groups to call for similar restrictions across the Arctic and ultimately a global prohibition. The country’s parliament, Inatsisartut, voted unanimously last month to direct the government to introduce a phased ban covering ports, internal waters and territorial seas extending 12 nautical miles offshore. Discharges from open-loop scrubbers will be prohibited from July 1, 2027, followed by closed-loop and hybrid systems from July 1, 2029. The restrictions will require affected ships to switch to compliant fuels or retain scrubber wastewater onboard while operating in Greenlandic waters. “The decision by Greenland’s parliament to ban scrubber discharges is an important step towards cleaner shipping, and a clear signal for other countries to do the same,” said Kaare Press-Kristensen, senior advisor at Green Global Future. Sian Prior, lead advisor to the Clean Arctic Alliance, is urging the IMO to introduce a global ban, starting with the environmentally sensitive Arctic. Greenland’s decision follows Denmark’s prohibition on open-loop discharges in July 2025, with Sweden and Finland introducing similar measures. The move also goes beyond the 2025 OSPAR agreement, which mandates phased restrictions in ports and internal waters but currently only recommends extending them to territorial seas.

items.title: China’s property starts plunge to 2002 levels
items.original_title: China’s property starts plunge to 2002 levels
items.summary: China’s property construction collapse has taken new building starts back to levels last seen in 2002, raising fresh questions about the long-term outlook for iron ore and coking coal demand, even as dry bulk owners become increasingly bullish about freight markets. Research published today by Ursa Shipbrokers reveals that Chinese property starts have fallen by 74% since 2019, from 2.27bn sq m to just 588m sq m last year. The deterioration is continuing. In the first nine months of 2026, new starts totalled 340m sq m, down 25% year-on-year and almost 80% below the equivalent period in 2019. Ursa notes that although construction starts have returned to levels comparable with the early 2000s, the circumstances could scarcely be more different. Chinese iron ore imports actually increased 4.1% in the first nine months of 2026, reflecting greater reliance on overseas supplies, inventory accumulation and changing trade patterns. Dionysios Tsilioris, a researcher with Ursa, told Splash today that the historic link between Chinese property starts and capesize earnings has disconnected to a large degree. China’s traditional construction-led demand engine continues to deteriorate, but longer trading distances and shifting mineral supply chains are helping support freight markets. Whether those factors can continue offsetting China’s structural property slump is emerging as a central question for capesize owners.

items.title: The human breaking point at sea
items.original_title: The human breaking point at sea
items.summary: Shipping cannot keep demanding more from less, argues Steven Jones, the founder of the Seafarers Happiness Index, in this strident exclusive for Splash. We are entering an extraordinary era of maritime technology. AI, autonomous ships, digital twins and sensors promise to transform shipping. The index, drawing on seafarers’ own accounts, fell to 6.81/10 in Q3 from 6.87 in Q2, continuing a decline from 7.26 in the last quarter of 2025. When people become exceptionally good at coping, organisations and industries can become exceptionally comfortable with the conditions they endure. One Captain describes manageable workloads at sea, followed by cargo operations, inspections, regulatory requirements and paperwork converging in port, while the office presses for shorter turnarounds. The Seafarers Happiness Index describes extraordinary commitment, but that should not be allowed to reassure us too much. A system can appear successful precisely because the people within it are absorbing its failures. We cannot keep demanding more from less and assuming resilience will fill the gaps.

items.title: Russia to sell $180m stake in Sovcomflot
items.original_title: Russia to sell $180m stake in Sovcomflot
items.summary: Russia is preparing to sell a 7.8% stake in state-controlled shipping giant Sovcomflot as Moscow searches for additional revenues to plug its growing budget deficit. The country’s Federal Agency for State Property Management, Rosimushchestvo, has launched a tender to select an adviser to organise the sale of 7.8% minus one share in the Moscow-listed tanker and LNG carrier owner. Applications close on November 17, with the proposed disposal valued at approximately RUB15bn ($184m) based on recent share prices. The Russian government currently controls 82.8% of Sovcomflot, having floated 17.2% of the company in 2020. Sovcomflot shares fell nearly 4% on Tuesday following the announcement, amid concerns that a placement of this size could require a substantial discount. Sovcomflot reported a first-half net profit of $284m, reversing a $435m loss a year earlier. Time-charter-equivalent revenues jumped 61% to $809m, while EBITDA more than doubled to $547m. The company remains subject to US, EU and UK sanctions over its role in transporting Russian energy exports. Moscow is also considering selling a 20% stake in Novorossiysk Commercial Sea Port and nearly 24% of Aeroflot as it seeks funds amid mounting expenditure on the war in Ukraine.

items.title: Samudera taps Yangzijiang yards for boxship duo
items.original_title: Samudera taps Yangzijiang yards for boxship duo
items.summary: Singapore-listed Samudera Shipping Line has ordered two containerships in China, adding 6,000 teu of capacity to its newbuilding pipeline. The Indonesian-controlled carrier disclosed in a filing that it had signed shipbuilding contracts with Jiangsu New Yangzi Shipbuilding and Jiangsu Yangzi-Mitsui Shipbuilding, both part of the Yangzijiang Shipbuilding group. The two vessels are scheduled for completion by 2030, with Samudera describing the contracts as part of its wider fleet development programme aimed at strengthening its container shipping operations. The company did not disclose the contract value, propulsion specifications or how the two vessels are allocated between the yards. The latest investment follows Samudera’s move into smaller feeder newbuildings through its Japanese venture with Imoto Corporation. In August, the jointly owned Blue Ocean Shipping contracted a 696 teu containership at China’s Zhejiang Xinle Shipbuilding, with that vessel scheduled for 2028. The Japanese venture, established earlier this year, is majority-owned by Samudera and has been expanding its presence in domestic and regional feeder shipping.

items.title: TS Lines adds $246m boxship brace in China
items.original_title: TS Lines adds $246m boxship brace in China
items.summary: Taiwanese liner operator TS Lines has returned to Shanghai Waigaoqiao Shipbuilding (SWS) for another pair of containerships in a deal worth $246m. The Hong Kong-listed carrier has contracted two 11,000 teu vessels at the CSSC-controlled yard, together with China Shipbuilding Trading, paying $123m apiece. The ships are scheduled for delivery in 2030, with the investment to be financed through internal resources and bank borrowings, according to a filing with the Hong Kong Stock Exchange. The latest order adds to a sizeable newbuilding programme TS Lines has been assembling across Chinese yards, covering both feeder and larger containership tonnage. In March, the company signed up for four 2,900 teu ships at Fujian Mawei Shipyard for $168.6m, with deliveries scheduled by May 2029. The deal followed a two-ship contract at the same yard in November 2025, taking that series to six vessels. TS Lines has also been building up its larger ship fleet at Waigaoqiao, where it previously contracted two methanol dual-fuel 14,000 teu vessels and two 7,092 teu ships. Founded in 2001, TS Lines operates primarily in intra-Asia trades. At the end of June, its fleet comprised 47 vessels with a combined capacity of nearly 140,000 teu, including owned and chartered tonnage.

items.title: Hormuz Oct crossings at 3-month high despite attacks, Red Sea traffic also rises
items.original_title: Hormuz Oct crossings at 3-month high despite attacks, Red Sea traffic also rises
items.summary: Strait of Hormuz shipping traffic rose to its highest monthly level since July in October, supported by stronger dry-bulk and LNG movements despite a decline in VLCC traffic and mounting regional threats, S&P Global Commodities at Sea(opens in a new tab) data showed Nov. 2. The rise came amid an “increasingly volatile” operating environment at Hormuz and the Bab al-Mandab Strait, with “reported projectile strikes, vessel fires and other security incidents” throughout October, CAS said. Despite elevated security risks over the month, observed and assumed Hormuz traffic totaled 750 transits in October, up from 749 in September, as VLCC traffic fell to 156 transits in October from 184 the previous month, but the declines in crude tanker transits were more than offset by other vessel classes, according to the CAS report. LNG carrier crossings, which fell steeply since Qatar LNG production units suffered damage at the start of the Iran war, also climbed, reaching 32 transits, or their highest since the start of the war. The Iranian authority had listed 240 vessels as violating its Strait of Hormuz transit guidelines and previously threatened non-compliant vessels with fines, seizure or confiscation. In the Red Sea, Bab al-Mandab traffic rose to 1,196 transits in October from 1,154 in September, while tanker movements were stable at 408 versus 404, CAS reported.

items.title: Alternative fuels need infrastructure: Why gas bunker vessels matter
items.original_title: Alternative fuels need infrastructure: Why gas bunker vessels matter
items.summary: The maritime industry is entering a period of growing fuel diversity. While much of the discussion focuses on fuels, engines, and regulations, the transition will also depend on the infrastructure needed to supply alternative fuels safely, reliably, and at scale. DNV’s new white paper, Gas bunker vessels – Facilitating the transition to alternative fuels, details how gas bunker vessels are becoming a critical part of that infrastructure and analyses the key factors shaping their future development, from market growth and vessel design to safety, operational readiness, and the adoption of emerging fuels such as ammonia. According to DNV’s Alternative Fuels Insight platform, around 900 LNG-fuelled vessels are now in operation worldwide, excluding LNG carriers. “Our analysis suggests the global LNG bunker vessel fleet may need to more than double by 2030, with between 165 and 208 vessels potentially required worldwide. Meeting that demand will require coordinated investment across the entire bunkering value chain, not just in the vessels themselves.” Gas bunker vessels emerge as a key link in the alternative fuel value chain The report argues that gas bunker vessels should be viewed as more than fuel delivery assets. While gas bunker vessels share many characteristics with conventional gas carriers, their role as fuel suppliers creates a distinct operating profile.

items.original_title: TT-Line expands use of automation in its fleet, selects Valmet to supply marine automation system to two new Green Ship 2.0s
items.summary: TT-Line, one of Europe’s leading ferry operators, has selected Valmet to deliver marine automation systems for two new Green Ships 2.0 that are currently being built at China Merchants Jinling Shipyard. The automation systems will help TT-Line to improve vessel efficiency, support reliable operations, reduce energy consumption, and advance its long-term decarbonization targets across Baltic Sea routes. The order continues the successful cooperation between TT-Line and Valmet following the installation of Valmet’s automation systems for the award-winning Nils Holgersson and Peter Pan ferries. By unifying the automation platform across its fleet, TT-Line can standardize operations, simplify maintenance, and support consistent vessel performance throughout the ships’ lifecycle. The new 240-meter Green Ship 2.0 ferries are designed to carry 1,000 people and feature LNG-hybrid propulsion combined with battery systems and are capable of using shore power. In addition to the onboard systems, TT-Line will benefit from Valmet’s lifecycle services, including remote support, maintenance services, software upgrades, training, and spare parts availability. “We are proud to continue our cooperation with TT-Line as it invests in a new generation of energy-efficient ferries. The project further strengthens Valmet’s position as a supplier of mission-critical automation for the marine industry. The order is included in Valmet’s orders received for the fourth quarter of 2026.

items.original_title: Chinese Penetrate South Korea’s LNG Carrier Market
items.summary: Chinese shipbuilders secured approximately 40% of all newly ordered large liquefied natural gas (LNG) carriers worldwide during the first to third quarters of this year, January to September. While China leads in the general merchant ship market, such as container ships and bulk carriers, by leveraging price competitiveness, large high-value-added LNG carriers with a capacity of 174,000 cubic meters or more were considered a market dominated by South Korean shipbuilders, who possess differentiated technology. Chinese shipyards have aggressively penetrated this sector this year. However, Chinese shipyards have recently entered the LNG carrier market one after another, beginning to accumulate experience and engaging in a “long-term battle.” Until 2021, only Hudong-Zhonghua Shipbuilding in China could construct large LNG carriers. As the first Chinese company to build and deliver a large LNG carrier in 2008, it grew by securing 36 orders out of 128 LNG carriers ordered by Qatar during its mass LNG production drive from 2020 to 2024, excluding those secured by South Korean shipyards. Over the past four years, four additional Chinese shipyards—Jiangnan Shipyard, Dalian Shipbuilding Industry, Yangzijiang Shipyard, and China Merchants—have entered the LNG carrier market. Jiangnan Shipyard delivered its first 175,000 cubic meter-class LNG carrier to a shipowner in November 2024, while Dalian Shipyard did so in September of last year, already accumulating shipbuilding experience.

items.title: Limpet Mines Return to the Gulf as Iran Strikes Four Tankers Near the Strait of Hormuz
items.original_title: Limpet Mines Return to the Gulf as Iran Strikes Four Tankers Near the Strait of Hormuz
items.summary: Between October 29 and 30, Iran attacked at least four tankers across the Strait of Hormuz and the waters around it. The attacks ranged from projectiles to hull-mounted explosives, and they struck laden and empty vessels, Qatari- and UAE-owned tonnage, and tankers that had spent weeks operating dark. Iranian sources separately claimed that four tankers hit mines in the Strait and caught fire, but it is unclear whether they were referring to additional vessels beyond the four confirmed. Projectiles Strike a Laden LNG Carrier Inside the Gulf On October 30, AL MAYEDA (IMO 9397298), a Marshall Islands-flagged, Qatari-owned LNG carrier, laden with an unknown quantity of LNG according to Vortexa, was struck by three projectiles around 18:00 UTC, approximately 40 nautical miles south of Lavan Island. AL MAYEDA had previously been dark between September 27 and October 30, and crossed inbound through the Strait of Hormuz during that period. Limpet Mines Return to the Gulf The same day, a small boat approached LOUISE 1 (IMO 9290323), a Panama-flagged, Panama-owned crude oil tanker, approximately 25 nautical miles northeast of Khasab, Oman, and emplaced two explosive devices on its hull. Why the Return of Limpet Mines Matters This latest round of attacks continues the trend established this month while expanding the methods Iran is using.

items.title: Japan Revives Shipbuilding with New LNG Dock
items.original_title: Japan Revives Shipbuilding with New LNG Dock
items.summary: Japan has embarked on a full-scale revival of its shipbuilding industry. To resume the construction of liquefied natural gas (LNG) carriers, the country is establishing a new large-scale dock for the first time in 18 years, and it is reactivating halted shipbuilding lines in response to defense budget increases and naval vessel export expansion. The prospect is that cooperation and competition between the shipbuilding industries of South Korea and Japan will intertwine, as Japan seeks technological cooperation with South Korean shipbuilders on LNG carriers while simultaneously emerging as a competitor in naval vessel exports. According to Japanese media such as the Nihon Keizai Shimbun and the Asahi Shimbun, Namura Shipbuilding will construct a new large-scale dock capable of building LNG carriers and other vessels in Imari Bay, Saga Prefecture by 2035. This marks the first time a new dock for large vessels has been built in Japan since Imabari Shipbuilding’s Marugame Headquarters in 2017. The Imari Works already possesses a large dock measuring about 450 meters in length and about 70 meters in width, but the company determined that additional production capacity is necessary as high utilization rates continue due to increased shipbuilding demand.

items.title: Wärtsilä completes milestone marine sector project to reduce methane emissions on vessels
items.original_title: Wärtsilä completes milestone marine sector project to reduce methane emissions on vessels
items.summary: Technology group Wärtsilä has successfully completed the conversion of one engine on three LNG carriers operated by Chevron Transport Corporation from dual-fuel (DF) to spark gas (SG) operation. This conversion aims to lower greenhouse gas emissions from the vessels by reducing methane slip, un-combusted methane that can escape into the atmosphere from LNG fuel. Following the successful conversion of these first three vessels, three additional vessel conversions are planned for execution later this year and next year, bringing the total number of converted vessels to six. This project represents a technical collaboration within the marine sector focused on addressing methane emissions from LNG-fueled vessels. Wärtsilä has successfully completed the conversion of one engine on three LNG carriers operated by Chevron Transport Corporation from dual-fuel (DF) to spark gas (SG) operation. © Chevron Shipping The Spark Gas Conversion for the Wärtsilä 50DF engine minimises methane emissions by introducing an electrically controlled pre-combustion chamber valve. The estimated result is that, on an IMO weighted (E2-cycle) average, the conversion reduces methane emissions down to 1.1 percent of fuel use. The solution is available to vessels in the industry with existing Wärtsilä 50DF engines for diesel-electric propulsion, the majority of which are LNG carriers.

items.summary: The Australian Maritime Safety Authority (AMSA) has banned a Marshall Islands-flagged bulk carrier from Australian ports for 90 days after inspectors discovered that crew work and rest records had been deliberately falsified to conceal excessive working hours. The ban against the Wooyang Venus follows an October 29 port State control inspection in Newcastle prompted by a complaint under the Maritime Labour Convention (MLC). Inspectors found that the vessel’s records did not accurately reflect the hours worked by its crew. According to AMSA , the Wooyang Venus was detained in August 2026 after inspectors found that crew work and rest hours were not being properly recorded or monitored. The vessel was also detained in December 2023 over incorrect work and rest records. AMSA said the 90-day ban was imposed under Section 246 of Australia’s Navigation Act 2012, citing the deliberate falsification of records, repeated deficiencies and concerns about the effectiveness of the vessel owner’s and operator’s safety management systems. Australian authorities have launched an investigation after the 182,066-dwt bulk carrier Cape Falcon ran aground off the Port of Gladstone, Queensland, with efforts to refloat the vessel so far unsuccessful. items.title: Poland has EU’s second-highest electricity prices accounting for cost of living
items.original_title: Poland has EU’s second-highest electricity prices accounting for cost of living
items.summary: Poland had the second-highest household electricity prices in the European Union in the first half of 2026 after adjusting for differences in the cost of living, new Eurostat data show. In nominal terms, Polish households paid €29.99 per 100 kilowatt-hours (kWh) for electricity in the first half of 2026. However, when adjusted for purchasing power standards (PPS), which account for differences in the cost of living, Poland ranked second in the EU, at 41.12 PPS per 100 kWh. One reason why electricity prices in Poland remain high is the country’s continued reliance on coal, which last year generated just over half of power , by far the highest proportion in the EU. These costs contribute to the high taxes and levies included in household electricity bills, which accounted for 39% of the final price in Poland in the first half of 2026. Without taxes and levies, the nominal price of electricity in Poland would have been just under €16 per 100 kWh, below the EU average of €20.27.

items.title: Upswing in domestic demand gives railfreight operators a revenue boost
items.original_title: Upswing in domestic demand gives railfreight operators a revenue boost
items.summary: Union Pacific led the way on the North American containerised rail freight front over the three months to October, amid all the noise surrounding its pending acquisition of Norfolk Southern – but it was not alone in enjoying a bountiful summer. In general, North American intermodal operators benefited from an upswing in domestic freight demand and a continuing tightening in the trucking market, with revenues up for all four of the major carriers. Boasting a 27% year-on-year revenue increase, Union Pacific took home some $1.52bn over the quarter, with volumes up 11%, to 956,000 carloads, and pointing specifically to reduced trucking capacity as behind the gains. “We’re very optimistic about the opportunities as we close this year and go into next on the domestic intermodal side,” she told investors, adding that the tightening in trucking could prove a boost when yields come up for renewal. Not one to miss out, Canadian Pacific Kansas City (CPKC) also reported double-digit revenue growth in intermodal, up 22% year on year to $583m, as volumes rose 9%, to 489,800 carloads. Together with the increased traffic, stronger pricing likely played its part in driving the improvement for the Canadian operator that saw its revenue per carload increase 12% year on year, to $1,190.

items.title: Norway Detains Sanctioned Chinese Vessel Over False Flag Registration
items.original_title: Norway Detains Sanctioned Chinese Vessel Over False Flag Registration
items.summary: Norway has detained a Chinese-owned heavy-lift vessel sanctioned for its role in delivering equipment to Russia’s Arctic LNG 2 project, in what appears to be the first known detention in the Arctic of a Chinese vessel linked to Russia’s shadow fleet. The Ya Qing Hai Yang was detained after Norwegian inspectors found that it lacked valid flag-state registration and required certificates, the Norwegian Maritime Authority said. The case is a notable enforcement action against a vessel with documented ties to Russia’s sanctioned energy sector, although authorities say the detention was based on maritime safety and registration deficiencies rather than the ship’s sanctions status. “During the inspection, it was discovered that the vessel did not have a valid flag registration and lacked the required certificates,” Dag Inge Aarhus, the authority’s communications director said last week. “The vessel has therefore been detained until further notice.” The vessel remains off the Vesterålen Islands as of November 3. The ship must establish valid registration with a flag state and obtain the necessary certificates before Norwegian authorities can complete the inspection and consider its release. The detention appears to be the first publicly documented case of Norway holding a vessel sailing under an invalid flag registration. The United States sanctioned the vessel’s operator and related entities in January 2025 .

items.title: Dronemaker Stark Designs Uncrewed Ship to Hunt Russia’s Shadow Fleet
items.original_title: Dronemaker Stark Designs Uncrewed Ship to Hunt Russia’s Shadow Fleet
items.summary: Nov 3, 2026 (Bloomberg) –German startup Stark Defence plans to launch a 24-meter uncrewed surface vessel next year, marking an expansion beyond small drones to more closely resemble an established defense contractor. The Berlin-based company’s new ship is designed to guard undersea cables and track Russia’s shadow fleet in European waters, Stark’s Chief Executive Officer Uwe Horstmann announced at Bloomberg Tech London on Tuesday. “Those are systems that cost a thousandth of the price of a manned frigate, which takes years to produce,” Horstmann said. Stark plans to develop the Vanta 24 in the UK and Germany, and hired Stephen Brian, a former nuclear submarine commander for the British Royal Navy, to run the company’s naval operations. He described Vanta 24 as a versatile vessel designed to escort warships or surveil on its own, replacing the labor-intensive work of monitoring coastlines and subsea cables. In June, it reached a valuation of €3.2 billion ($3.6 billion) and has grown to more than 700 employees. Luciana Lixandru, a partner with Sequoia Capital, said the Silicon Valley investor backed Stark because it believes the company will be one of Europe’s few defense newcomers to compete with prime contractors.

items.original_title: Major liners set to resume all Asia-Europe services through Suez
items.summary: All the mainline operators look set to resume Suez Canal transits for their Asia-North Europe and Asia-Mediterranean services. Taiwan’s Evergreen will join its Ocean Alliance partners in doing just that this week, while Yang Ming and South Korea’s HMM will join their Premier Alliance partners restarting Suez crossings next month. Linerlytica’s report today says Evergreen will send the 16,556 teu Ever Eon and Ever Edit on eastbound Suez transits on the Ocean Alliance’s NEU7/CES service on 7 and 11 November, respectively, with the 20,124 teu Ever Gifted on the alliance’s MD2 service on 16 November. The Premier Alliance’s Asia Mediterranean 1 (MD1) service will resume Suez transits next month, adding a new call at Sokhna to cater for Asia-Red Sea cargo. In recent months, vessel capacity constraints, and competitive pressures following a temporary easing of regional security risks, have convinced shipping lines to resume Suez crossings. HMM’s spokesperson told The Loadstar South Korea’s flagship carrier had assessed the risks before deciding to resume Suez transits.

items.title: Fears a strike at San Pedro Bay ports could worsen congestion
items.original_title: Fears a strike at San Pedro Bay ports could worsen congestion
items.summary: Concern is rising among cargo owners and logistics providers that a strike at the Los Angeles/Long Beach port complex could turbo-charge the congestion there. About 250 watchmen, who perform security-related duties at container terminals at the twin ports, are poised to walk off the job at 5pm Pacific time on Wednesday, should last-minute contract negotiations between the International Longshore and Warehouse Union (ILWU) and the Pacific Maritime Association (PMA) fail to reach agreement. Watchmen have been working under contract extensions since the agreement expired in July 2025. Union members had authorised a strike for 1 November, but both sides agreed to extend negotiations until 4 November. According to the PMA, a work stoppage would affect 85% of the container traffic at the port of Long Beach and 33% at Los Angeles. Ted Chen, ocean freight and trade compliance director at logistics provider Dimerco, said there was a high likelihood that other port employees would support the strike, a concern echoed by forwarder Woodland Group. The actual scale of any interruption would depend on the terminals affected, the participation of other workers and the duration of industrial action.” ,Moreover, the disruption would aggravate congestion that has resulted in extended dwell times for rail cargo at several of the affected terminals.

items.title: Offshore operators should not wait for EU ETS clarity to act on emissions data
items.original_title: Offshore operators should not wait for EU ETS clarity to act on emissions data
items.summary: EU MRV has applied to offshore vessels of 400 GT and above since 1 January 2025, and vessels of 5,000 GT and above are scheduled to enter the EU ETS from the 2027 reporting period. On 17 July 2026, the European Commission published proposals that would revise the MRV framework from 1 January 2029 and bring offshore vessels between 400 and 5,000 GT into the ETS from 2031. These are not final, however, and must still pass through the legislative process. The International Marine Contractors Association (IMCA) has welcomed the recognition of offshore-specific terminology and operational realities, but says more clarity is needed on ports of call, cross-border operations and how the EU and UK ETS interact. In August, Norway’s Ministry of Climate and Environment confirmed that FuelEU Maritime and ReFuelEU Aviation, previously expected to take effect later this year, will not enter into force for Norway before 1 January 2028. From 2029, companies operating on the Norwegian continental shelf must reduce the greenhouse gas intensity of ships used in oil and gas activity, starting at 10% for 2029-2031 and rising in stages to 40% for 2038-2040. Rystad Energy estimates close to 300 offshore vessels fall within scope, and that most of them, including LNG dual-fuel units, would miss the first threshold based on how they operate today.

items.title: Ernst Russ offloads another feeder in fleet reshuffle
items.original_title: Ernst Russ offloads another feeder in fleet reshuffle
items.summary: German shipowner Ernst Russ has sold another feeder containership, continuing to trim its older boxship exposure while building up its tanker and multipurpose fleet. The Frankfurt-listed company has confirmed the sale of the 2007-built, 803 teu Mirror , without disclosing the buyer and price. The vessel is expected to change hands in January 2027. The disposal follows the sales of EF Emira and EF Emma earlier this year, extending a fleet reshuffle that has seen the Hamburg-based owner move further beyond its traditional containership business. Mirror was among six feeder vessels in which Ernst Russ bought out its joint venture partners’ holdings in October last year, part of a drive to simplify the group’s ownership structure. In September, it added another two 18,500 dwt chemical and product tanker newbuildings at China’s Wuhu Shipyard, increasing the programme to six vessels. Both additional ships were fixed to commodities group Cargill for at least three years, adding approximately $38.3m to contracted charter revenue. That followed an initial four-tanker acquisition in April, with the two packages together generating around $164m in contracted charter backlog. Ernst Russ has also expanded into modern multipurpose tonnage, acquiring two heavylift vessels earlier this year on seven-year charters to dship Carriers.

items.title: Singapore VLSFO back above $1,000 for first time since March
items.original_title: Singapore VLSFO back above $1,000 for first time since March
items.summary: The cost of fuelling ships has climbed back above $1,000 a tonne in Singapore for the first time since March, as the prolonged Iran conflict continues to drive up bunker bills across the global merchant fleet. Data from Ship & Bunker show very low sulphur fuel oil (VLSFO) broke through the $1,000 threshold on October 28, reaching $1,000.50 a tonne. Prices subsequently climbed to $1,019.50 on Friday before easing to $1,003.50 on Monday. Ship & Bunker data show Singapore VLSFO was trading at $521.50 a tonne immediately before the conflict. The fuel has since increased by more than 92%, having reached a peak of $1,120.50 on March 13. For a ship taking on 3,000 tonnes of VLSFO, the current bunker bill is approximately $3m, compared with $1.56m before the war, an additional $1.45m for a single stem. Scrubber-equipped vessels retain a significant advantage, with the Singapore VLSFO-HSFO spread currently standing at $105 a tonne. According to bunker pricing specialist ENGINE, LNG bunkers in Singapore reached $1,939 a tonne on Monday, up $74 over the previous week. Ship & Bunker assessed Rotterdam VLSFO at $763.50 a tonne on Monday, around $240 below Singapore, while Fujairah was quoted at $991.50.

items.title: Grimaldi lines up 10 car carrier newbuilds in China
items.original_title: Grimaldi lines up 10 car carrier newbuilds in China
items.summary: Italian shipping group Grimaldi is lining up another 10 car carriers at Chinese shipyards, including a series of 11,000 ceu vessels that would become the largest in its fleet. The Naples-based owner has signed letters of intent with China Merchants for five next-generation 10,000 ceu pure car and truck carriers (PCTCs) and with CSSC’s Guangzhou Shipyard International (GSI) for another five ships of 11,000 ceu each. Both designs will have additional capacity for containers and other rolling cargo, extending their capabilities beyond conventional vehicle transportation. The latest move builds on Grimaldi’s extensive car carrier expansion in China. In 2022 and 2023, the group amassed an orderbook of 17 ammonia-ready PCTCs (pictured), comprising 10 ships at China Merchants and seven at CSSC-affiliated yards. The proposed 11,000 ceu series would take Grimaldi another step up in vessel size, while adding greater flexibility to carry a combination of vehicles, containers and other roro cargo. The car carrier projects form part of a wider fleet investment programme valued at more than €4bn ($4.5bn). Grimaldi has also commissioned a tenth ropax ferry at China Merchants Jinling Shipyard in Weihai for its Spanish subsidiary Trasmed, involving an investment of €160m ($179m).

items.title: MINSHIP and Oskar Wehr launch joint shipmanagement venture
items.original_title: MINSHIP and Oskar Wehr launch joint shipmanagement venture
items.summary: German shipping companies MINSHIP and Oskar Wehr have launched a joint shipmanagement venture, BellRock Maritime, with an initial fleet of 12 vessels and ambitions to expand into third-party management. The company commenced operations yesterday, combining the partners’ technical management, crewing and QHSE activities from offices in Hamburg and Schnaittenbach, Bavaria. The partners each hold 50% of the venture, with five ships contributed by MINSHIP and seven by Oskar Wehr. Klehr has served as managing director of Oskar Wehr alongside third-generation family boss Thomas Wehr since 2006. Founded in 1945, Oskar Wehr has a history of collaborating with other German owners. In 2019, it joined Nordic Hamburg and Bertling to establish OneBulk, a commercial management platform for handysize bulk carriers. MINSHIP’s predecessor businesses date back to 1985. BellRock will be led operationally by fleet director Lasse Grundmann, previously with Oskar Wehr. Both shareholders will retain their independent commercial shipping operations, while the new company seeks additional technical and crew management contracts from outside owners.

items.title: Ports falling further behind shipping’s alternative fuel revolution
items.original_title: Ports falling further behind shipping’s alternative fuel revolution
items.summary: Ports are failing to keep pace with the extraordinary growth in alternative-fuel ship orders, raising the prospect of a two-tier global bunkering network where large parts of the merchant fleet struggle to obtain the fuels their vessels were designed to burn. A new 65-page report from Lloyd’s Register (LR), Fuel for Thought: Ports, reveals that 1,942 alternative-fuel-capable ships were on order at the start of 2026, representing 47% of global orderbook tonnage. The latest figures from rival class society DNV show the total number of alternative-fuelled vessels ordered in 2026 to 364, 57% higher than over the same period in 2025. Yet LNG bunkering was available at just 222 ports worldwide, methanol at 25, while commercial ammonia bunkering had been recorded at only one port by the report’s September research cut-off. Splash Ports reported in September that the International Association of Ports and Harbors fears an increasingly divided port system, with developing countries requiring between $55bn and $83bn for climate adaptation and decarbonisation. The economics remain challenging, with green methanol and ammonia costing two to three times conventional marine fuels, despite cargo owners being willing to pay average premiums of just 3%. Splash reported in October that European grid upgrades could take four to 10 years, threatening ports’ ability to meet mandatory connection requirements from 2030.

items.title: Stefanou brothers snap up modern capesize from Oldendorff
items.original_title: Stefanou brothers snap up modern capesize from Oldendorff
items.summary: The Stefanou brothers have snapped up their youngest capesize to date, paying just under $50m for the 2017-built, 179,120-dwt William Oldendorff . The Jinhai-built vessel is a rare find, with only a handful of modern capesizes changing hands this year. The Greek owners have firmly committed to the second hand market this year, having already added a 2009-built conventional panamax and two kamsarmaxes, built in 2011 and 2017, this year. The brothers operate through two bulker arms, Bright Navigation and Sea Gate Navigation, which together control more than 30 bulkers with an average age approaching 20 years if one combines the two companies as one. Their existing three capesizes rank among the oldest ships in the fleet, making the latest purchase a clear renewal play. The deal comes amid firm capesize earnings where it could easily fix the ship out for around $35,000 per day on a one-year deal.

items.title: When the ship pays back before the owner does
items.original_title: When the ship pays back before the owner does
items.summary: Fuel-saving retrofits can pay for themselves long before the shipowner who funded them sees a return. A new BIMCO contract seeks to resolve shipping’s longstanding divide between who pays for efficiency and who pockets the savings. Alex Byelyavtsev reports. If the owner pays to burn less, the immediate fuel saving shows up first in the charterer’s accounts. If the charterer pays, the steel stays on someone else’s ship when the fixture ends. If the owner funds the whole amount and keeps half of that saving, the owner’s simple payback stretches to about 4.9 years. Yet the owner would have recovered only $1.44m, leaving $910,000 still unrecovered when the fixture ended. The ship can reach payback before the investor does. Under BIMCO’s ETS clause for time charter, the charterer provides and pays for the allowances corresponding to the vessel’s emissions during the charter period.

items.original_title: MABUX: Global Bunker Market To Maintain A Firm But Highly Volatile Trend In November
items.summary: October’s global bunker market remained under strong geopolitical and supply-side pressure. Middle East tensions, disruptions to oil product flows, tight regional fuel availability and rising LNG prices continued to support bunker quotations. • Middle East Conflict: Continued instability around the Strait of Hormuz sustained elevated geopolitical risk premiums, freight costs and bunker price volatility. The upward trend in bunker prices during October was primarily driven by the continued escalation of the military conflict between the United States and Iran, which sustained a substantial geopolitical risk premium in global crude oil and refined petroleum product prices. The MABUX Global Scrubber Spread (SS) – the price differential between 380 HSFO and VLSFO – continued its moderate downward trend in October, declining by USD 5.94, from USD 140.59 at the end of September to USD 134.65, while remaining above the USD 100.00 SS Benchmark. We expect the SS Spread to maintain a moderately downward trend in November, although geopolitical developments and bunker fuel price volatility may continue to influence market dynamics. Meanwhile, the European natural gas benchmark TTF recorded a sharp increase in October, surging by EUR 24.650/MWh, from EUR 73.938/MWh in September to EUR 98.588/MWh.

items.title: Fuel Switch Snapshot: Pooling slump erases LBM’s edge over LNG
items.original_title: Fuel Switch Snapshot: Pooling slump erases LBM’s edge over LNG
items.summary: Liquefied biomethane (LBM) has flipped from a $2/mt discount to LNG to a $48/mt premium over it in Rotterdam for vessels with Otto medium speed (Otto MS) engines. For vessels with diesel slow speed (diesel SS) engines, it has flipped from a $6/mt discount to a $43/mt premium. OceanScore’s FuelEU pooling index has fallen by €15.35/mtCO2e ($17/mtCO2e) to €80.45/mtCO2e ($90/mtCO2e) over the past week. This has cut the potential pooling value of LBM’s compliance surplus by $53-62/mt on intra-EU voyages, against $0-9/mt for LNG. LBM prices have gained $133-141/mt depending on engine type, and LNG prices $84-92/mt over the past week. The lower potential pooling value of LBM’s compliance surplus has added to the rise in LBM prices and undercut their edge over LNG. LSMGO has slid in Rotterdam while both gaseous fuels have climbed, flipping its premiums of $73/mt over LNG (diesel SS) and $79/mt over LBM (diesel SS) to discounts of $94/mt and $137/mt. Rotterdam’s LBM prices have climbed by $133-141/mt depending on engine type over the same period. Singapore’s LNG prices have risen by $63-67/mt depending on engine type.

items.title: Scarce tonnage creates two-speed ship recycling market, says Wirana
items.original_title: Scarce tonnage creates two-speed ship recycling market, says Wirana
items.summary: A widening gap between ship recycling markets across the Indian subcontinent is showing that local yard appetite, financing conditions and available capacity are increasingly influencing vessel values independently of regional steel-price movements, according to Wirana Shipping. In Bangladesh, the shortage of recycling candidates and strong demand from yards are encouraging recyclers to bid above the levels supported by local steel-market fundamentals. The number of facilities holding a Document of Authorisation to Conduct Ship Recycling (DASR) or Conditional DASR has risen to 39, increasing competition for the limited tonnage entering the market. Ship recyclers subsequently reduced their offers by approximately USD 15–20/MT, while interest in the limited dry bulk candidates being circulated remained weak. Rakesh Khetan, CEO of Wirana Shipping, said: “Ship recycling is not moving as a single regional market. Bangladesh recyclers are bidding above local steel-market fundamentals because tonnage is scarce and yard appetite is strong, while Pakistan is being pulled in the opposite direction by weak steel demand and abundant imported material. Wirana expects overall recycling supply to remain slow in the immediate term. However, steam-turbine LNG vessels and smaller dry bulk ships could provide the next source of recycling candidates as charter-market conditions change. Source: Wirana Shipping Corporation

items.title: The ETS investment engine: scaling Europe’s strategic e-fuel market for shipping and aviation
items.original_title: The ETS investment engine: scaling Europe’s strategic e-fuel market for shipping and aviation
items.summary: The EU Emissions Trading System (ETS) review proposal published in July 2026 is intended to make the EU’s most vital climate policy mechanism fit for its 2040 climate targets. It also carries the ambition to turn the ETS into an ‘’engine for innovation and investment”. This policy brief looks at the investment dimension of the ETS proposal with respect to the aviation and maritime sectors. The ETS Review is an opportunity to set up a tailor-made investment tool to de-risk and boost the production and uptake of e-fuels, using the ETS funds from aviation and shipping. • 1 Use national ETS revenues: earmark 50% of national ETS revenues for decarbonisation support in priority sectors, including for the production and uptake of aviation and maritime e-fuels, and ensure compliance via stricter reporting rules. • 2 EU-level ETS funds: include aviation and maritime sectors in the scope of the ETS Investment Booster, Industrial Decarbonisation Bank (IDB) and Modernisation Fund to enable e-fuels support and ensure equity across hard-to-abate sectors. • 3 Create an e-fuels funding pool: channel ETS revenues and other funding sources to finance a market intermediary for e-fuels by 2028.

items.title: Slowing Intra-Asia Chemical, Palms Spot Freight Fixtures Deter Trades
items.original_title: Slowing Intra-Asia Chemical, Palms Spot Freight Fixtures Deter Trades
items.summary: Tanker freight in Asia beating popular expectations by staying buoyant into November could hinder chemical and palms cargo flows throughout the rest of the fourth quarter. • Liquid bulk shipping costs climb despite fleet growth • El Nino supply jitters prolong palms freight uptick • Tanker pile-up at ports curtails SE Asia, India tonnage supply Freight indications having already advanced since September have further increased into November despite new vessel additions and pre-Diwali holiday restocking in India tapering off. During the two-week period to 28 October, ICIS-assessed chemical and palms freight indications have risen on most intra-Asia trade lanes. Unlike for palms freight, supply-demand forces tied to regional chemical trades have been mixed, thus far reflected in uneven freight indications across trade lanes. Active gasoline blending trades are still bolstering southbound chemical freight indications, which continue to outperform those for northbound, intra-southeast Asia and intra-northeast Asia trade lanes. “Freight [for liquid bulk] is a headache now [especially] for part parcel cargoes,” a trader active in southbound trades separately lamented during the week ended 28 October. Back then, shipping veterans had suggested that with newbuild tankers entering service hitting multi-year high, liquid bulk freight, including for chemical and palms shipments, should come under pressure in 2026.

items.title: Alternative fuels comprised 12% of NYK’s marine fuel mix in 2025
items.original_title: Alternative fuels comprised 12% of NYK’s marine fuel mix in 2025
items.summary: Low greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions marine fuels accounted for 12.2% of Japanese shipping company NYK Line’s total fuel consumption in the financial year 2025 (FY2025). Japanese shipping company Nippon Yusen Kabushiki Kaisha (NYK Line) continued to expand its dual-fuel fleet, operating 35 such vessels in the previous financial year, up from 26 in 2024. The figures exclude LNG carriers and LNG-ready vessels, the company said. Biofuels comprised the largest share of NYK Line’s marine fuel mix during the mentioned period, followed by LNG. Biofuel consumption rose to 297,000 mt in FY2025, continuing an upward trajectory from 251,000 mt a year earlier and a baseline of 6,000 mt in FY2023. The shipping company is actively “increasing the use of biofuels and alternative fuels available today to achieve immediate GHG emissions reductions.” NYK Line’s progressive shift toward low-emission marine fuels helped the company to reduce its emissions by 260,000 mt of CO2 equivalent (CO2e) in FY2025, it said. The shipping company laid a groundwork for broader biofuel adoption with the launch of a 12-month B100 (100% biofuel) pilot project aboard a car carrier in May 2026. “In addition to the B100 trial, NYK is advancing the evaluation and verification of Cashew Nut Shell Liquid (CNSL) as part of efforts to expand the range of sustainable biofuel options,” it said.

The capesize index, which typically transports 150,000-ton cargoes, including iron ore and coal, slipped nearly 4% to 3,963 points, after three consecutive sessions of advances. At the same time, the panamax index, which usually carries 60,000 to 70,000 tons of coal or grain, decreased by 0.8% to its lowest since April 13 at 1,874 points, extending its losing streak to 14 consecutive sessions. items.title: Could India’s steel ‘Vision 2047’ create the next breakthrough for dry bulk demand?
items.original_title: Could India’s steel ‘Vision 2047’ create the next breakthrough for dry bulk demand?
items.summary: On 10 October 2026, the government released the draft National Steel Policy: Vision 2047 for public consultation, with ambitious targets. The vision projects steelmaking capacity to surge from the current 220 million tonnes to 604 million tonnes by 2047, while crude steel production is expected to reach 531 million tonnes (up from 164 million tonnes in 2025). The policy also projects annual iron ore demand of 772 million tonnes, coking coal demand of 236 million tonnes and scrap consumption of 123 million tonnes. India’s crude steel production For dry bulk shipping, the key question is not whether India can produce more steel. We previously estimated that the corridor could support more than 90 million tonnes of annual exports and generate demand for 70-80 Capesize vessels. Australia is likely to remain India’s largest supplier, but rising imports from Canada, the US and Mozambique could create additional opportunities for both Capesize and Panamax vessels. At the same time, growing scrap requirements could create an additional import market. Even though China will remain the world’s largest iron ore importer for the foreseeable future, its steel market is increasingly mature.

items.title: Ardmore Shipping: Decarbonization through the details
items.original_title: Ardmore Shipping: Decarbonization through the details
items.summary: The regulatory requirements governing environmental performance continue to ratchet up, with the EU Emissions Trading System in place for large ships entering EU ports since January 2024, FuelEU Maritime in effect since January 2025 and the IMO’s Carbon Intensity Indicator tightening. At the same time, negotiations continue over the IMO’s Net Zero Framework. For us, however, efficiency is a long-term operating discipline, not a reaction to each new rule. At year-end 2025, we had 26 product and chemical tankers in operation and our latest Sustainability Report identifies 13 diverse energy efficiency technologies in use on our vessels, from Mewis Ducts and propeller boss cap fins to variable speed drives and low-load boiler optimization, as well as DeepSea’s AI-enabled voyage optimization, and weather-routing services from WetterWelt, all of which combine to support more fuel-efficient operations across the fleet. Seafarers can access on-demand training through the AFLIX app, use virtual reality to familiarize themselves with vessels before joining, and provide anonymous peer feedback on safety competencies through our Safety Rating app. What’s more, our WAVES initiative, which supports women at sea, helped grow our community of women officers from 16 to 25 in 2025. As regulatory requirements evolve, we will keep improving vessel efficiency through practical investment, informed decision-making and the expertise of our people.

items.title: Broad Industry Coalition Urges Permanent Suspension of Costly U.S. Port Fees on China-Linked Ships
items.original_title: Broad Industry Coalition Urges Permanent Suspension of Costly U.S. Port Fees on China-Linked Ships
items.summary: A broad coalition of maritime, agricultural, manufacturing, retail and logistics organizations is urging the Trump administration to permanently suspend U.S. port fees targeting China-linked vessels, warning that reinstating the charges would raise costs for American businesses, hurt exporters and disrupt global supply chains. In an October 30 letter to U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer , the coalition welcomed the proposed two-month extension of the Section 301 vessel fee suspension through January 9, 2027, but called on Washington to go further and eliminate the charges permanently. Because Chinese-built ships account for a significant share of global shipping capacity, the coalition warned that the impact would extend well beyond Chinese shipping companies, affecting vessel deployments and transportation costs for American importers and exporters. The coalition also challenged the idea that port fees would meaningfully rebuild America’s struggling commercial shipbuilding industry. The latest industry appeal follows the Trump administration’s October 23 proposal to extend the suspension through January 9, 2027, as Washington and Beijing continue negotiations over China’s dominance of the maritime, logistics and shipbuilding sectors. The push for a permanent suspension comes amid competing pressure from lawmakers and maritime labor unions, which argue that the fees are necessary to counter China’s state-supported shipbuilding industry and encourage investment in American shipyards.

items.title: Imported iron ore margin narrows to 0.04 yuan/mt
items.original_title: Imported iron ore margin narrows to 0.04 yuan/mt
items.summary: The average imported iron ore margin narrowed from 8.72 yuan/mt to 0.04 yuan/mt in the latest period, weighed down mainly by lower port spot prices and higher freight. Iron ore currently faces rising supply and falling demand. The latest SMM data showed iron ore stocks at 35 major ports across China at 148.05 million mt, up 300,000 mt from the previous survey, marking a slight build. Average daily port outbound volume fell 35,000 mt to 3.175 million mt. Iron ore fundamentals remain bearish. With hot metal output expected to decline further next week, iron ore demand may continue to weaken, capping upside for prices. Macro factors also lack a stronger driver, and prices are expected to remain range-bound next week. The import margin is likely to narrow gradually in the short term as freight rates rise. Source: SMM

items.title: UAE to Protect Energy Infrastructure, Invest in New Export Routes to Prepare for Iran War, Minister Says
items.original_title: UAE to Protect Energy Infrastructure, Invest in New Export Routes to Prepare for Iran War, Minister Says
items.summary: United Arab Emirates' Minister of Energy and Infrastructure, Suhail Mohamed Al Mazrouei attends the opening ceremony of the annual Abu Dhabi International Petroleum Exhibition and Conference (ADIPEC) in Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates, November 2, 2026. REUTERS/Amr Alfiky ABU DHABI, Nov 2 (Reuters) – The UAE will protect its energy infrastructure and invest in new export routes, storage capacity abroad and shipping fleets to be better prepared for the US-Israeli war on Iran, its energy minister said on Monday. Minister Suhail al-Mazrouei said the course of the war could not be predicted, but the UAE would be more prepared than before. It is building a new pipeline to Fujairah that will double crude capacity by next year. “I think after this crisis, many companies are going to look, think again, and design, redesign their facilities to be more resilient in the future,” Mazrouei told reporters on the sidelines of the Abu Dhabi International Petroleum Exhibition and Conference. Reuters had reported in June that the UAE boosted crude oil and condensate exports to a record high , shortly after it left the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries.

items.title: JB Hunt faces data breach lawsuits as hackers claim haul of carrier records
items.original_title: JB Hunt faces data breach lawsuits as hackers claim haul of carrier records
items.summary: Companies that have faced a cyber attack are now increasingly likely to face lawsuits too, from customers or staff over any breach of data security. JB Hunt is the latest: it is facing four proposed class actions, after a cybercrime group claimed to have taken employee information and millions of business records from the US transport and logistics company. The suits, filed in the Western District of Arkansas on 27 and 28 October, allege JB Hunt failed to protect employees’ personal information. The JB Hunt attacker, calling itself WhiteArmor, posted its claim on or about 23 October, although it is not clear exactly when the hack took place. The complainants repeat its claim to hold 140,838 employee records for a $5m ransom. One complaint also lists what WhiteArmor claims to hold: 1.7m carrier contacts, 38.2m invoices, 973 Microsoft 365 mailboxes, and records concerning 374,000 organisations. Aaron Hunter, a former employee, said in his complaint that he had received no individual breach notice as of 27 October , when he filed his complaint. Following a 2022 cyber attack that shut down most of Expeditors’ operating systems, customers including iRobot and POC USA sued the forwarder over alleged losses from interrupted warehousing and deliveries.

items.title: China and Russia are redrawing Arctic trade. Can Europe fight back?
items.original_title: China and Russia are redrawing Arctic trade. Can Europe fight back?
items.summary: China and Russia are tightening their grip on Arctic shipping routes, turning the rapidly warming region into a new geopolitical battleground with Europe. Moscow and Beijing last week have agreed to expand freight traffic along Arctic shipping corridors, increase services between their ports and deepen cooperation on building polar vessels. The agreement came after the EU unveiled a new Arctic strategy aimed at countering growing Russian and Chinese influence in the region. Cargo traveling between Asia and Europe through the Northern Sea Route could have its journey shortened to between 18 to 22 days, down approximately 35% from the 28 to 35 day journey through Suez, according to data provided by Fertmax FZCO. “The significance of the arctic route is for Russian energy shipments to China, which will increase China’s control over Russia in terms of Russia’s dependence on China to sell its energy to compensate for losses of its gas markets in Europe,” Roche highlighted. ‘’With Russia and China increasing their footprint and ambition, the Arctic has become a front line of global power competition.’’ Kaja Kallas Foreign Policy Chief, European Union The EU’s new strategy calls for expanding European icebreaker capacity, strengthening maritime surveillance and developing infrastructure linking Arctic trade networks to European markets.

items.title: Chinese ship-owner CMES holds vessel-naming ceremony in South Korea, advancing the two countries’ shipbuilding cooperation
items.original_title: Chinese ship-owner CMES holds vessel-naming ceremony in South Korea, advancing the two countries’ shipbuilding cooperation
items.summary: The first vessel under China Merchants Energy Shipping’s (CMES) second-phase LNG project with QatarEnergy was named in South Korea on October 28-29, according to media reports, marking progress in cooperation between Chinese ship-owners and South Korean shipbuilders. The LEKHRAIB, the first of six 174,000-cubic-meter LNG carriers ordered by CMES from South Korea’s Samsung Heavy Industries (SHI), was named during ceremonies held on Geoje Island and in Busan. The vessel will provide long-term LNG transportation services for QatarEnergy. In addition to the six vessels built by Samsung Heavy Industries, CMES secured long-term transportation contracts for four larger 271,000-cubic-meter QC MAX carriers, which are being built by China’s Hudong-Zhonghua Shipbuilding. LNG carriers are among the most technologically demanding commercial vessels, as they transport natural gas at temperatures of around minus 162 C. The LEKHRAIB features a GTT Mark III Flex membrane containment system, with a designed daily boil-off rate of no more than 0.085 percent, as well as dual-fuel engines. South Korean shipbuilders have long held a strong position in large LNG carrier construction, while Chinese shipyards have been expanding their capabilities and securing more orders for advanced vessels, Wang Peng, an associate researcher at the Beijing Academy of Social Sciences, told the Global Times.

items.title: Asia Break Bulk adds heavylift muscle in Schoeller deal
items.original_title: Asia Break Bulk adds heavylift muscle in Schoeller deal
items.summary: Singapore-based Asia Break Bulk has secured four 12,600 dwt multipurpose heavylift newbuildings through a long-term deal with Schoeller Holdings. The COLI Group-controlled carrier said the Octopus-type vessels, designed by China’s CSSC-SDARI, will feature two 250-tonne cranes capable of tandem lifts of up to 500 tonnes. The first ship is scheduled for delivery in October 2028, with the remaining three to follow. The vessels will have a single box-shaped cargo hold measuring more than 89 m in length, while a forward-mounted superstructure will provide additional deck space for oversized cargo. Asia Break Bulk, which marks its 20th anniversary this year, has traditionally operated semi-liner services connecting Asia and Europe. Maximilian Fischer, general manager at Asia Break Bulk, said customers are increasingly looking for shorter transit times and direct access to ports with draft restrictions, reducing the need for costly and time-consuming transshipments. Schoeller Holdings is backing the newbuilding programme, while Columbia Shipmanagement will supervise construction and take over technical and crew management once the vessels enter service. The deal adds another chapter to Cyprus-based Schoeller’s extensive investment in multipurpose and heavylift tonnage. Earlier this year, the group booked two 32,000 dwt MPP vessels at China’s CSSC Huangpu Wenchong Shipbuilding for delivery in 2029, extending a relationship with the yard dating back to 2008.

items.summary: UK diversified shipowner Union Maritime has added two more 24,200 dwt product tanker newbuildings at China’s Dalian Shipbuilding Offshore Co (DSOC), taking its programme at the yard to six vessels. The Laurent Cadji-led company’s updated fleet list identifies the additional ships under hull numbers PC24K-5 and PC24K-6, both scheduled for delivery in 2028. No contract value has been disclosed. The latest additions build on a four-ship contract placed with the restructured Dalian yard in January 2025. Those vessels were estimated at about $30m apiece, putting the original programme at roughly $120m. The company’s current schedule has three of the earlier ships down for 2026 and the fourth for 2027. Union Maritime’s website now lists 81 newbuildings, up from the 79 recorded in September, when the London-based owner added another nine vessels across five segments. That expansion included two newcastlemax bulkers at Wuhu, two MR product tankers at Jingjiang Nanyang, an LR2 at Guangzhou Shipyard International, a chemical tanker pair in Japan and two handysize bulkers at Imabari. The privately held owner has also moved into large gas carriers through orders in China and South Korea.

items.title: Hijacked fishing vessel approaches shipping lane amid Somali piracy fears
items.original_title: Hijacked fishing vessel approaches shipping lane amid Somali piracy fears
items.summary: Commercial shipping in the western Indian Ocean has been warned of a potential new piracy threat after armed attackers seized an Iranian fishing vessel off Somalia and moved it towards a busy maritime traffic lane. The Azini was hijacked on Thursday, October 29, off the northeastern Somali coast, with 21 Iranian crewmembers and two Somali security guards aboard. According to a Puntland Maritime Police Force officer, 12 pirates boarded the vessel between Bandar Bayla and Hafun. The captain reportedly managed to send a distress voice message to another vessel before communications were lost. The Maritime Security Centre – Indian Ocean (MSCIO) subsequently tracked the vessel moving eastwards, with its latest reported position at 09°47’N, 055°45’E, approaching a commercial shipping route. Maritime security authorities are particularly concerned that the fishing vessel could be used as a mothership, allowing pirates to launch attacks against merchant ships hundreds of miles offshore. The seizure comes amid a worrying resurgence of piracy around Somalia. According to the Associated Press, six commercial vessels had been hijacked between April and August. In September, Puntland security forces recovered the tanker Honour 25 after a lengthy hijacking, with five crewmembers reportedly killed during the incident.

MSC’s operated fleet stood at approximately 7.47m teu at the end of October, with its newbuilding pipeline approaching 3.4m teu, according to Alphaliner figures. The combined capacity of ships in service and on order has now passed 10m teu. Waigaoqiao has meanwhile secured several large boxship programmes from other major liner operators.

items.title: Hormuz attacks spread deeper into the Gulf
items.original_title: Hormuz attacks spread deeper into the Gulf
items.summary: Commercial shipping has come under renewed attack in and around the Strait of Hormuz over the weekend, with tankers and an LNG carrier targeted as Washington and Tehran exchange increasingly belligerent warnings despite fresh diplomatic efforts to end the eight-month conflict. In the latest incident, a tanker sailing southeast through the Arabian Gulf was struck by two unidentified projectiles on its port side, 72 nautical miles east of Saudi Arabia’s Ras Al Khafji late on Sunday. UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) reported that all crew were accounted for, with no pollution reported. Maritime security firm Vanguard Tech identified the ship as the UAE-owned offshore tug Selat Storm, reporting that it was partially sinking. The crew’s condition remains unclear. The vessel remains operational and its crew is safe. Doha condemned the attack and launched an investigation. The vessels have not been identified and the claims remain unverified. Splash reported last week that Iran had singled out South Korean tanker giant Sinokor for enforcement action against its fleet from November 1.

items.title: Russia moves to bar ageing foreign ships from its ports
items.original_title: Russia moves to bar ageing foreign ships from its ports
items.summary: Russia has formally put proposed restrictions on ageing merchant ships out for public consultation, seeking to bar foreign-flagged vessels older than 40 years from its ports as Moscow tightens oversight of the fleet carrying its seaborne trade. The transport ministry published the draft legislation, proposing a separate 50-year threshold for Russian-flagged ships, with transitional arrangements tied to the validity of their classification certificates. Foreign-flagged vessels older than 30 years would also face annual inspections to confirm compliance with safety and environmental requirements. The proposed rules would assess vessels against their inspection and repair records, technical condition and insurance coverage. Cargo transportation contracts would also have to specify the use of compliant ships, while marine terminal operators would assume additional responsibilities for ensuring vessels meet the requirements. The move advances an initiative Moscow has been developing for more than a year. The transport ministry outlined the proposed 40-year limit for foreign ships in July, alongside plans for tighter oversight of older Russian tonnage. However, the government faces a substantial fleet replacement challenge. Deputy transport minister Alexander Poshivay said last month that restrictions would not be adopted until the country was confident replacement vessels could be secured, acknowledging that domestic shipyards face constraints on capacity, pricing and construction times.

items.title: Ningbo Ocean maps $1.5bn eight-ship leasing expansion
items.original_title: Ningbo Ocean maps $1.5bn eight-ship leasing expansion
items.summary: China’s Ningbo Ocean Shipping is preparing another major fleet expansion, unveiling plans to lease eight new vessels under agreements carrying potential rental commitments of up to RMB10.3bn ($1.53bn). The Shanghai-listed carrier said the proposed programme covers four 7,000 teu containerships, two 14,000 teu vessels and two 7,000 ceu pure car and truck carriers, with lease periods of up to 20 years. The largest vessels would mark a significant step beyond Ningbo Ocean’s traditional feeder and regional container operations, while the car carrier pair would further strengthen its push into vehicle shipping. The company has set maximum cumulative rental commitments of RMB3.9bn ($581m) for the four 7,000 teu ships, RMB4bn ($596m) for the larger containership pair and RMB2.4bn ($357m) for the two car carriers. The figures represent maximum payments over the life of the leases, including possible purchase payments at expiry, rather than shipbuilding contract prices. Ningbo Ocean has yet to identify financing partners, yards or vessel delivery dates. The board approved the proposal last week, but shareholder approval and final contracts are still required. The Ningbo-Zhoushan Port-controlled company entered the car carrier market in August through a chartered 7,000 ceu vessel operating between China and Europe. It has also been expanding its containership orderbook at Chinese yards, including Wuchang and Huangpu Wenchong.

items.original_title: Maritime CEO Forum: Dry bulk owners eye generational rate rally
items.summary: Dry bulk shipping could be approaching a generational freight rate rally as surging West African mineral exports transform tonne-mile demand, according to shipowners speaking at last week’s Maritime CEO Forum in Monaco, although concerns remain over the rapid expansion of Chinese shipbuilding capacity. John Michael Radziwill, chairman of CTM, argued that 2026 had exceeded expectations and that geopolitical disruption was proving supportive of freight markets. “I think we’re probably on the cusp of a generational rate rally,” he told the session, moderated by Mandarin Shipping chairman Tim Huxley, pointing out that dry bulk had yet to experience the extraordinary earnings witnessed in other shipping sectors since 2021. At Geneva Dry six months ago, expectations were for Simandou exports of 45m tonnes next year. The dry bulk orderbook remains relatively manageable at around 16% of the existing fleet, rising to approximately 19% for capesizes, according to Pappas. Pappas cited modern kamsarmax sales at $44m to $45m and capesize resales exceeding $90m. D’Amico questioned the economics of paying $46m for a 66,000 dwt ultramax, calculating that it would need to earn more than $18,000 daily over 20 years. Asked where they would invest today, d’Amico favoured people and operational improvements over additional ships, while Radziwill revealed CTM had acquired 12 vessels since May.

items.title: Muscat charts maritime resilience framework
items.original_title: Muscat charts maritime resilience framework
items.summary: Asyad Group, the end-to-end logistics solutions flagship of the Sultanate of Oman, is seeking to develop what it describes as the world’s first fully integrated maritime resilience framework, bringing international industry leaders together to establish practical priorities for safeguarding supply chains and sustaining global trade amid mounting operational and commercial pressures. The proposed Muscat Maritime Resilience Framework is the central initiative of the Muscat Maritime Resilience Forum 2026, which opened on Tuesday with discussions on strengthening maritime networks, improving preparedness and translating industry experience into coordinated action. The commercial stakes were highlighted by an Asyad operational study showing a 137 per cent variation in the total cost of a maritime voyage between India and Suhar. Speaking at the opening, Asyad Group Chief Executive Abdulrahman bin Salim al Hatmi said the framework would draw on the expertise of maritime leaders and practitioners to address challenges affecting costs, business continuity and commercial operations. “For the first time, international maritime leaders and practitioners are coming together in Muscat to contribute to the development of what we intend to be the world’s first-ever, fully integrated maritime resilience framework,” he said.

items.title: Offshore Industry Sends Urgent Call To EU Policymakers For Fit-For-Purpose EU ETS And MRV Framework
items.original_title: Offshore Industry Sends Urgent Call To EU Policymakers For Fit-For-Purpose EU ETS And MRV Framework
items.summary: Eight maritime associations including the Royal Belgian Shipowners’ Association (KBRV) send an open letter to EU policymakers urging them to ensure a fit-for-purpose framework for the European offshore sector under the current EU ETS review. The offshore shipping sector is a strategic asset to the European economy, playing a leading role in the continent’s energy transition, energy security and industrial competitiveness. Yet the current EU ETS framework, entering into force beginning 2027 for offshore vessels, will distort competition and create opportunities for circumvention, based on a Monitoring, Reporting, and Verification (MRV) framework that was not designed for offshore operations and is widely recognised as not fit for purpose. The sector strongly urges EU policymakers to first ensure that a fit-for purpose activity-based MRV framework is operational, before the inclusion of offshore vessels above 5000GT in EU ETS from next year onwards. Below is the open letter the sector has addressed to the European Parliament and members of the Council EU ETS REVIEW: GET THE FRAMEWORK RIGHT FOR EUROPE’S OFFSHORE SECTOR Open letter to Members of the European Parliament and EU Member States’ Permanent Representatives.
